meta.title: Hermeneutic of ecclesial continuity
meta.notice: This is a research layer written for this site. It applies a published method to disputed texts and records where the method succeeds, where it fails and where the evidence is not yet in. Its verdicts, confidence levels and the proposed synthesis on Constance, Basel and Vatican I are scholarly hypotheses, not teaching of the Catholic Church and not a judgment of any office of the Holy See.
plain: A text of the Church can be truly binding and still not be permanent. A law, a penalty, a pastoral rule or a prudential judgment binds while it is in force, and competent authority can later change it, because it was a determination for a time and a set of circumstances.

A definition is different. What the Church has proposed definitively cannot later be denied in the same sense. So the first question about any apparent reversal is what kind of act each text is, and what exactly it proposed.

Two texts conflict only if they say opposite things about the same subject, in the same sense, at the same time and in the same circumstances. Often they do not; sometimes they do. Where a real conflict remains after honest reading, this site says so instead of explaining it away.

Non-definitive teaching asks religious submission of mind and will, and the Church herself says such teaching can contain deficiencies (Donum Veritatis 24). How far divine assistance protects it is a theological question, which this site treats as open.
evidence_review: Record the witness and how it is known. Distinguish the enacted text, contemporary testimony, a draft, a later interpretation and a citation still to verify.

State the claim the evidence supports or weakens. For a contested legal act distinguish the fact of the act, the competence to perform it and the scope of its reception. If an act was revoked as a precaution, establish its prior force independently.
Compare the strongest rival explanations against the same evidence. Record the missing premise and what evidence could change the conclusion.
Rerun the conditions and comparisons. If the method itself changes, give the reason and retain the previous assessment alongside the new one.

formal_object.revealed: Revealed doctrine: proposed as divinely revealed.
formal_object.definitive: Definitive doctrine: proposed to be held definitively, connected with revelation.
formal_object.juridical: Juridical norm: a law, statute or canonical rule.
formal_object.moral_application: Moral application of a principle to circumstances.
formal_object.judicial: Judicial sentence: a judgment on persons or a case.
formal_object.dogmatic_fact: Dogmatic fact: a fact so connected with doctrine that the Church judges it.
formal_object.disputed: Disputed: what kind of claim this is, is itself the question.

assent.religious_submission: Religious submission of mind and will (canon 752; Lumen Gentium 25).
assent.obedience: Legal obedience to a law or precept while it is in force.
assent.prudential_deference: Respect and deference to a prudential judgment; reasoned disagreement possible.
assent.none: No assent is owed: a private opinion, a witness or a historical record.
assent.disputed: The grade of assent is itself disputed.

binding_status.not_juridical: Not a juridical act: legal force does not apply.
binding_status.in_force: A law or act in force now.
binding_status.lapsed: Was in force; has lapsed by disuse, fulfilment or change of circumstance.
binding_status.abrogated: Was in force; revoked or replaced by competent authority.
binding_status.annulled: Declared null from the start by competent authority.
binding_status.never_in_force: Never had legal force (no competent authority).
binding_status.disputed: Whether and how it bound is disputed.

evidence.D: Established doctrinal statement: what a magisterial text plainly says or defines.
evidence.H: Documented historical fact, with a source.
evidence.T: Defensible theological interpretation, held by recognised theologians.
evidence.N: Novel theory proposed on this site.
evidence.U: Unresolved claim: the evidence is not yet in or does not decide it.

verdict.demonstrated_concord: Demonstrated concord: every critical premise verified.
verdict.plausible_concord: Plausible concord: a substantial case, with a live objection.
verdict.unresolved_tension: Unresolved tension: the method has not reconciled the texts, or the research is incomplete.
verdict.textual_conflict_requires_revision: Textual conflict: the texts conflict as they stand; a reading or a classification must be revised.
verdict.not_comparable: Not comparable: different genre or subject.

matrix_result.no_conflict: No conflict: the propositions differ in subject, sense, scope or time.
matrix_result.apparent: Apparent conflict, removed by the reading given.
matrix_result.potential_contradiction: Potential contradiction: conflict if both are read in the sense stated.
matrix_result.contradiction: Contradiction: P and not-P in the same sense.
matrix_result.undetermined: Undetermined: depends on a premise not yet established.

stages: Open the complete primary text; verify the original language and, where possible, a critical edition; record citation and provenance.
Extract atomic propositions, with their qualifications and the text of any censure or condition.
Identify authority, genre, formal object, jurisdiction, grade of assent and binding status, each separately.
Record the controversy, tacit assumptions, confirmation, reception, later substitution or repeal, and current debate.
State rival propositions in identical logical terms (subject, quantifier, modality, time, circumstance) in a contradiction matrix.
Ask whether a legitimate determination, changed facts or different qualifications explain the change. Not an escape for opposite immutable moral claims.
Distinguish explanation and qualification from reversal; name the definitive content that survives.
For pope and council conflicts, apply the seven pass conditions; otherwise record "not applicable".
State the strongest evidence-based objection, with citations, and a fair rebuttal, or admit failure.
Confidence, evidence gaps, unanswered objections and the next most probative source.
A reader's summary, the detailed research, the opposing view, citations and labels for hypotheses.

benedict.source: Benedict XVI, Address to the Roman Curia, 22 December 2005
benedict.status: An address, not a magisterial definition. It is used here as the method, not as a ruling on any of the cases below.
benedict.summary: Benedict XVI asked why the reception of the Second Vatican Council had been so hard, and answered that two hermeneutics had been at odds. A hermeneutic of discontinuity and rupture reads the Council as a break, and looks for its true "spirit" beyond its texts, as if a council were a constituent assembly that could give the Church a new constitution. A hermeneutic of reform, of renewal in the continuity of the one subject Church, reads the Council as the same Church, growing and developing while remaining the same. Taking religious liberty as his example, he said that in the Church's concrete decisions on contingent matters there can be discontinuity, while continuity remains at the level of principle; recognising this is part of true reform.

rules.title: One enduring ecclesial subject
rules.text: No council is a constituent assembly empowered to replace the divinely given constitution of the Church.

rules.title: Separate principles from contingent expressions
rules.text: The same principle may generate different determinations under genuinely changed historical and juridical conditions.

rules.title: Permit correction of historical decisions
rules.text: Authentic reform may revise earlier concrete decisions without reversing the principles that motivated them.

rules.title: Prove continuity at the correct level
rules.text: Name the principle that actually continues; repeating the words "continuity" or "development" proves nothing.

rules.title: Respect the textual form
rules.text: The "spirit" of a document cannot override what the document says; an alleged historical qualification needs evidence.

benedict.inference_note: Where a case below applies these rules to Constance, Basel, the Jansenist condemnations or any other dispute, the application is this site's inference from Benedict's method, not his judgment on that dispute. He gave one worked example, religious liberty (case B1).

principles.title: Logical and propositional precision
principles.rule: Extract the exact subject, predicate, scope, modal force, qualifications, time and object of each claim. P and not-P conflict only when asserted in the same sense and circumstances; two time-bounded commands can differ without asserting contradictory universal doctrines.
principles.guards: Treating two texts as contradictory because their words clash, before their subjects, scopes and times are compared.

principles.title: Documentary priority and competence
principles.rule: Identify original language, critical text, date, promulgator, session, procedural status, confirmation, reception and repeal. Inclusion in Denzinger or omission from it is editorial evidence, not a doctrinal ruling.
principles.guards: Arguing from a translation, a summary or an editor's selection as if it were the act itself.

principles.title: Formal-object differentiation
principles.rule: Tag each claim as revealed doctrine, definitive doctrine, authentic non-definitive teaching, juridical norm, pastoral determination, moral application, judicial sentence, dogmatic fact, historical assertion or private opinion. One act can mix several.
principles.guards: Giving a whole document the weight of its weightiest sentence, or of its lightest.

principles.title: Proportionate assent and obligation
principles.rule: Distinguish divine and Catholic faith, definitive assent, religious submission of mind and will, legal obedience and prudential deference. Binding force, factual correctness, doctrinal truth and irreformability are four different properties.
principles.guards: Concluding from "this bound" that "this is irreformable", or from "this was changed" that "this never bound".

principles.title: Contingent determination under permanent authority
principles.rule: The divinely instituted power to bind and loose can ground real obligations that are neither uniquely best nor permanent (Aquinas's determinatio, applied by analogy). No human law can abrogate divine law. The analogy of an executive order illuminates governance, not the truth of competing doctrinal propositions.
principles.guards: Using "it was only discipline" to dissolve a claim the text proposes as true; or treating every law as an eternal truth.

principles.title: Homogeneous development
principles.rule: Show how a later clarification or qualification keeps the earlier definitive truth. Context must come from historical evidence; an exception may not be inserted simply because a contradiction would otherwise remain.
principles.guards: Calling any change "development", or any development "rupture".

principles.title: Indefectibility, infallibility and safety
principles.rule: Infallibility operates under defined conditions; indefectibility keeps the Church in the apostolic faith and constitution. A wider doctrinal safety (securitas doctrinalis) for non-definitive teaching is a theological theory, not a defined grade of the Magisterium. Donum Veritatis 23–31 admits limitations and deficiencies in prudential interventions.
principles.guards: Assuming that whatever was taught with authority must have been without error, or that whatever was not infallible may be ignored.

principles.title: Presumption of concord, with falsifiability
principles.rule: Seek a genuine historical reconciliation; state the best contrary interpretation; disclose any residual conflict. Never manufacture concord by reclassifying a plainly definitive claim as discipline or by leaving out difficult sentences. A failed or undetermined test stays visible.
principles.guards: Reaching the expected conclusion by changing the rules case by case.

levels.title: Logical
levels.test: Are the complete propositions truly P and not-P?

levels.title: Doctrinal
levels.test: Does later teaching preserve what was definitively taught?
levels.change: Formulation, development, clarification; not definitive negation.

levels.title: Juridical
levels.test: Was each rule valid during its own legal operation?

levels.title: Constitutional
levels.test: Does the one Church retain her divinely established offices?
levels.change: Extraordinary remedial arrangements, if independently justified.

gate.theory: Conditional extraordinary conciliar competence under a permanently Petrine constitution: a legitimately constituted general council might, under rigorously defined ecclesial emergencies, exercise a restorative competence immediately grounded in Christ, to protect the faith, to determine legitimacy in a schism, or to restore the lawful conditions of the Petrine office, without becoming a standing court superior to a certain and legitimate pope. This is novel and disputed; its existence and scope must be proved, not assumed.
conditions: Keep every definition of Vatican I intact.
Preserve real binding force for the early acts of Constance and Basel in their demonstrated sense.
Explain both the immediate, Christ-derived authority claimed and the resistance to papal dissolution.

Give an objective criterion for the emergency that a council could never invoke against a certain and peacefully accepted pope; show that the historical case met it under each rival account of which papal line was legitimate, and who convoked the council under each. A full procedure for future cases is not required.
Distinguish lawful amendment of contingent decrees from invalidation of their original authority.
Substantiate any limit placed on universal-sounding conciliar claims from their text and reception.
Answer a strong defender of Vatican I and a strong conciliarist without caricature.
gate.warning: Neither "Martin V confirmed everything" nor "Martin V rejected everything except individually confirmed acts" may be asserted as established fact without the exact text, a critical edition, a contextual reading and later corroboration. Omissions from Denzinger are not evidence of any office's judgment.
gate.rule: A failed condition means unresolved, not reconciled. D1 may never be marked demonstrated concord on the strength of a constitutional analogy alone.

history.text: Specify who discerns an emergency and who can convoke a legitimate council.
history.reason: Reworded in v0.3. The v0.2 wording asked the hypothesis for a working procedure for future emergencies. No received Catholic doctrine of an extraordinary case has one: the classical theologians never settled who declares a pope a heretic (Cajetan, Bellarmine, Suárez, John of St Thomas differ), and that doctrine is not thereby held incoherent. Requiring it of this hypothesis alone would break adversarial test 7. The condition keeps its purpose: without an objective criterion, any council could claim an emergency against a certain pope, which would rebuild the standing tribunal that condition 1 excludes. The v0.3 wording also requires the historical case to be tested under each rival account of the legitimate papal line. Disclosure: the rewording was made after D1 had failed under v0.2, and it can change D1's verdict; both verdicts are shown.

adversarial: Do we preserve the strongest wording of the earlier source?
Have we identified a principle that really continues, rather than inventing one?
Are later terms being read anachronistically into an earlier text?
Does "context" improperly convert universal moral teaching into local policy?
Is the conclusion dependent on a disputed papal confirmation or quotation?
Can an opponent accurately restate our conclusion without conceding our premises?
Would the same rules yield an unfavourable conclusion for a text we favour?
Has the site distinguished historical research from teaching promulgated by the Church?

cases.title: Cum occasione: what the five propositions condemn
cases.question: Does a condemnation attach to the literal wording of a proposition, to its sense in the author's system, or to every possible orthodox construal of the words?
cases.summary: Innocent X assigned a censure to each of five propositions on grace. The fifth calls it Semipelagian to say that Christ died for everyone. The bull calls that statement false, rash and scandalous and gives the note of heresy to the sense that Christ died for the salvation of the predestined alone. Trent teaches both that Christ died for all and that the benefit of his death is received by those to whom his merits are communicated. Alexander VII confirms the censures as given and declares that the propositions were condemned in Jansen’s intended sense. The distinction between a death genuinely for all and its particular application gives a basis for comparing accounts of the atonement. The first four propositions raise separate questions about prevenient grace, resistance and freedom.

texts.label: Innocent X, Cum occasione (31 May 1653)
texts.edition: Bullarium Romanum, Turin ed., XV (1868), pp. 720–722, especially §4 at p. 721.
texts.checked: Checked all five censures in Latin. In the fifth, dumtaxat limits the heretical sense to the claim that Christ died for the salvation of the predestined alone.

texts.label: Alexander VII, Ad sanctam beati Petri sedem (16 October 1656)
texts.edition: Bullarium Romanum, Turin ed., XVI (1869), pp. 245–247, §6. Also cited as Ad sacram.
texts.checked: The bull confirms the earlier constitution, identifies the intended sense of Jansenius and renews the censures with the same note assigned to each proposition.

texts.label: Paul V on the Congregatio de Auxiliis (1607)
texts.edition: Denzinger, n. 1090 (DS 1997), from the formula sent to both superiors on 5 September 1607.
texts.checked: The printed formula sends the disputants home and forbids either side to censure the other. It anticipates a later determination. Independent review of the source behind the printed formula remains open.

texts.label: Council of Trent, decree on justification (1547)
texts.edition: Session VI, chapters 3, 5, 11 and 15 and canons 4, 17 and 18.
texts.checked: Chapter 3 distinguishes death for all from the communication of its merits. Chapter 5 starts with prevenient grace and affirms free assent and the possibility of refusing it.

texts.label: Innocent X, decree on alleged acts of De auxiliis (23 April 1654)
texts.edition: Denzinger, n. 1097 (DS 2008), referring to Paul V and Urban VIII.
texts.checked: The decree printed in Denzinger disallows an alleged constitution condemning Molina and directs the parties to observe the decrees of Paul V and Urban VIII.

propositions.says: Proposition 1 (some commandments are impossible to the just who will and strive, the grace that would make them possible being lacking) is condemned as rash, impious, blasphemous and heretical.
propositions.note: The proposition includes the absence of the grace by which the precepts could be kept. Trent chapter 11 and canon 18 directly bear on that premise.

propositions.quote: In the state of fallen nature one never resists interior grace
propositions.says: Proposition 2 (in fallen nature interior grace is never resisted) is condemned as heretical.
propositions.note: This claim quantifies over all instances of interior grace. An account of how a particular grace infallibly brings about free consent is a different claim.

propositions.says: The bull censures as heretical the claim that freedom from coercion alone suffices for merit or demerit and that freedom from necessity is unnecessary.
propositions.note: Analyse what kind of necessity is claimed and whether it removes the agent’s freedom. The formula alone does not explain how assent can follow infallibly from a grace.

propositions.says: The bull calls the fourth proposition false and heretical. It claims that the Semipelagians held prevenient grace necessary even for the first movement of faith and were heretical for making that grace resistible.
propositions.note: Trent chapter 5 and canon 4 affirm both the necessity of prevenient grace and the possibility of refusal. The heresy cannot consist in affirming that the will can refuse grace.

propositions.says: The proposition calls it Semipelagian to say that Christ died for all without exception. Innocent X calls it false, rash and scandalous. In the sense that Christ died for the salvation of the predestined alone he also calls it impious, blasphemous, contumelious, injurious to divine goodness and heretical.
propositions.note: The Latin dumtaxat means alone or only. This word is part of the stated condition for the further censures.

propositions.quote: in the sense understood by that same Cornelius condemned
propositions.says: The propositions are taken from Jansen's Augustinus and condemned in the sense he intended.
propositions.note: Section 6 confirms the preceding constitution and renews each censure with its original theological note. The precise grade of the dogmatic fact is discussed in A2.

propositions.says: Paul V dismisses the disputants and forbids either side to attach a theological censure to the other’s position.
propositions.note: The 1607 formula reserves a later determination. Innocent X’s 1654 decree rejects the alleged constitution condemning Molina (1097).

propositions.says: Christ died for all. Those to whom the merits of his passion are communicated receive the benefit of his death.
propositions.note: Trent, session VI, chapter 3. Catechism §605 explicitly reiterates that Christ died for everyone and cites Quiercy.

propositions.says: The will moved by God can cooperate by assenting to his call and can refuse if it wills. The beginning of justification depends on prevenient grace (797).
propositions.note: Trent, session VI, chapter 5 and canon 4. Canon 17 rejects the claim that only the predestined to life receive justifying grace and that the rest are called without grace as if predestined to evil. Chapter 15 teaches that justifying grace, once received, can be lost.

matrix.why: Proposition 2 rules out resistance to every interior grace. A Thomist account of some graces as effecting free consent can affirm that other interior graces are resisted. The 1607 formula leaves the explanation of efficacy open.
Alexander VII confirms each original censure in the sense intended by Jansen. The additional censure in proposition 5 depends on the sense that Innocent X states, including the word alone.

The earlier Trent text states both universal death and particular communication of its benefits. The condemned sense excludes people from the saving scope of Christ’s death itself. Particular reception leaves that universal scope intact.
Trent affirms the priority of grace and the possibility of refusing it. Innocent X rejects the proposition that such resistibility was itself the Semipelagians’ heresy.

cases.qualifications: Innocent X assigns a censure to each proposition. The fifth receives three censures as stated and additional censures under its expressly stated restrictive sense.
cases.reception: Alexander VII confirmed the five censures and declared that the propositions were condemned in the sense intended by Jansen. The Jansenist distinction between doctrine and attribution is examined in A2.
cases.contingency: The censure and the duty to reject the condemned doctrine are doctrinal questions. The penalties imposed to enforce the constitution are juridical.
cases.development: Orange II and Trent teach the priority of grace for faith and justification. Trent affirms the reality of free cooperation, the possibility of refusing divine inspiration and the communication of Christ’s merits. Catechism §605 reiterates that Christ died for everyone.
cases.hypothesis: A genuinely universal atonement and a particular reception of its benefits agree with Trent and the fifth censure. This point can be shared by hypothetical universalism when it means that Christ’s death was truly offered for all. Its wider account of how grace is given and received must be tested separately.
cases.objection: A theory may grant that the sacrifice has infinite value while holding that it was offered only for the elect. It may also call reception conditional while restricting justifying grace to the finally predestined. Either move would affect the claimed agreement with Trent. On the grace side, an account of infallible efficacy still has to explain how the act remains free.
cases.rebuttal: The test is whether all are included in the saving scope of Christ’s death and whether receipt of its merits is a further claim. Davenant’s distinction between universal sufficiency by divine ordination and an application through faith illustrates that first distinction. Trent separately requires prevenient grace, real cooperation and the possibility of refusal. Canon 17 rejects the restriction of justifying grace to the predestined in the stated sense, and chapter 15 says that justifying grace can be lost. Infallible efficacy can be compared with the third proposition only after the proposed kind of necessity is identified.

research_sources.title: Catechism §605 on Christ dying for all
research_sources.role: Catechism with a citation of Quiercy
research_sources.citation: Catechism of the Catholic Church, §605, citing Quiercy (853), DS 624 (n. 319).
research_sources.note: The Catechism teaches that Christ died for all without exception. Quiercy also distinguishes his suffering for all from the salvation of all.

research_sources.title: John Davenant on a sacrifice actually offered for all
research_sources.citation: Dissertation on the Death of Christ, sect. 31 in the linked edition.
research_sources.note: Davenant distinguishes the unlimited worth of Christ’s sacrifice from its divine appointment as a remedy for all. In his example the price may be sufficient to pay every debtor’s debt and yet be offered for only some. His argument for universal sufficiency requires the offer to extend to all.

research_sources.title: Jansenius on Christ dying for all
research_sources.citation: Augustinus, Louvain (1640), vol. III, De gratia Christi Salvatoris III.21, especially cols. 381–382.
research_sources.note: Jansenius reports the explanation that Christ paid a sufficient price for all. He then says that offering a ransom for someone implies directing it to that person’s liberation, and the direction cannot be in vain. He reads all as the Church throughout the world, drawn from every kind of person.

evidence_reviews.question: What does the fifth censure say about the death of Christ for all?
evidence_reviews.finding: Innocent X calls the charge of Semipelagianism false, rash and scandalous. He calls it heretical in the sense that Christ died for the salvation of the predestined alone. Trent says he died for all and distinguishes that from the actual communication of his merits (795).
evidence_reviews.test: Ask whether a theory says that Christ’s death was truly offered for every person or whether it grants only that the price would have been enough. Examine separately how it says the benefits are applied.

evidence_reviews.question: How much does the comparison with hypothetical universalism establish?
evidence_reviews.finding: Davenant’s account of the sacrifice as a remedy ordained for all can agree with Trent on the scope of the atonement. Jansenius acknowledges the worth of the price and restricts the saving direction of the offering in his reading of all. Trent also teaches the priority of grace and that the will can assent or refuse. Its teaching on losing justifying grace and canon 17 bear on who receives that grace (808, 827).
evidence_reviews.test: Compare a particular author’s account of faith, justification and the offer and reception of grace with Trent. Agreement on the scope of the atonement establishes agreement on that point.

evidence_reviews.question: What remains open on the efficacy of grace?
evidence_reviews.finding: Trent affirms God’s prior action and the will’s real cooperation. Innocent X censures the denial of resistance to interior grace and the claim that freedom from coercion alone suffices for merit. Paul V forbids the two schools to censure each other on the disputed means of efficacy.
evidence_reviews.test: Distinguish a grace that can be resisted from the claim that an efficacious grace infallibly brings about a free act. Examine what kind of necessity is asserted and whether it removes the will’s agency.

cases.title: Ad sacram: the binding force of a dogmatic fact
cases.question: When Alexander VII declared that the five propositions are in Jansen's book and condemned in his sense, what kind of claim was that: a dogmatic fact, a historical fact, or a judgment derived from the first condemnation?
cases.summary: The dispute concerned two claims. Innocent X censured five propositions on grace and Alexander VII declared that they were taken from Jansenius’s Augustinus and condemned in his intended sense. The 1665 formulary required a sincere rejection of that sense. Clement XI ruled in 1705 that respectful silence fell short of the required obedience and called for rejection in word and heart. Theologians use the category of dogmatic fact for a judgment of fact bound up with doctrine. The 1998 commentary on the Profession of Faith illustrates that category. The precise grade of assent owed to this particular judgment is a further question.

texts.edition: Bullarium Romanum, Turin ed., XVI (1869), pp. 245–247, §6. Also cited as Ad sacram.
texts.checked: The bull confirms the earlier constitution, identifies the intended sense of Jansenius and renews the censures with the same note assigned to each proposition.

texts.label: Alexander VII, Regiminis apostolici and its formulary (1665)
texts.edition: Bullarium Romanum, Turin ed., XVII (1869), p. 336.
texts.checked: The formulary links the earlier bulls and requires the signatory to reject the five propositions with a sincere mind in the sense intended by their author.

texts.label: Clement XI, Vineam Domini (1705)
texts.edition: Bullarium Romanum, Turin ed., XXI (1871), pp. 233–236, especially §6, p. 235.
texts.checked: Section 6 demands interior rejection of the condemned sense and sincere subscription. Section 5 confirms the earlier constitutions.

texts.label: Doctrine of the Faith, commentary on the Professio fidei (1998)
texts.edition: Doctrinal commentary on the concluding formula of the Professio fidei, §11.
texts.checked: The commentary gives examples of truths connected to revelation by historical necessity. Its examples include canonisations and the legitimacy of an ecumenical council.

texts.label: Cornelius Jansenius, Augustinus on the scope of Christ’s death (1640)
texts.edition: Augustinus, Louvain (1640), vol. III, De gratia Christi Salvatoris III.21, cols. 381–382.
texts.checked: Jansenius first sets out the reading of all in terms of the sufficiency of the price. He then argues that offering redemption for a person directs it to that person’s liberation and that Christ’s offering cannot be in vain. He explains all as the Church drawn from every people.

propositions.quote: have been taken from the book of the aforementioned Cornelius Jansen
propositions.says: The five propositions are taken from the Augustinus and condemned in Jansen's sense.
propositions.note: The declaration’s demand for real assent is documented. The site leaves the exact theological grade of this particular judgment open.

propositions.says: A formulary of submission to both constitutions, to be signed by clergy and religious.

propositions.quote: is not satisfied by any obsequious silence
propositions.says: The obedience owed is not satisfied by respectful silence; the condemned sense of Jansen's book must be rejected in heart.
propositions.note: Clement XI confirms the earlier constitutions and requires rejection of the condemned sense. Read the fifth proposition with Innocent X’s express qualification and Alexander VII’s renewal of each censure.

propositions.says: The commentary gives examples of truths to be held definitively because of their historical connection to revelation. It refers to dogmatic facts and includes canonisations among the examples.
propositions.ext: Doctrine of the Faith, commentary on the Professio fidei, no. 11 (1998)

matrix.why: The commentary illustrates a class of historical judgments that can be definitive. Applying that class to this passage of Alexander VII requires evidence of the grade of the particular act.
The formulary is a juridical instrument that has lapsed; the teaching that interior assent is owed to such a judgment does not depend on it.

cases.qualifications: Ad sacram defines "in the sense understood by" Jansen; Vineam Domini speaks of "the sense of that book".
cases.reception: Fénelon and the anti-Jansenist theologians defended the Church's competence over dogmatic facts; Arnauld and Pascal denied it. Modern manuals treat dogmatic facts as a secondary object of infallibility, a thesis theologians call common but not defined.
cases.contingency: The formulary was a disciplinary measure and has lapsed. The judgment of fact is not contingent in that way.
cases.development: The category was clarified, not changed, by the 1998 commentary.
cases.hypothesis: Ad sacram is a judgment of dogmatic fact, binding with definitive assent according to the common theological reading, and consistent with the 1998 commentary. (T)
cases.objection: Whether a sentence is in a book, and in what sense its author meant it, is a historical question that revelation does not contain. To demand interior assent to it is to extend the Church's protection beyond faith and morals (P7). Modern historians also argue that some propositions are not verbatim in the Augustinus.
cases.rebuttal: Alexander VII affirms that the propositions come from the book and names Jansenius’s intended sense. Clement XI explicitly requires rejection of the condemned sense even in the heart. That establishes the practical obligation. How the propositions were formulated, where their sense is found in the book, and the precise theological grade of the attribution require their own evidence.

gaps.what: Jansenius’s text and the formulation of the remaining propositions
gaps.source: Augustinus (1640), the propositions submitted to Rome, and the examinators’ records.
gaps.settles: How the propositions reproduce or summarise Jansenius’s arguments. For the fifth, book III, chapter 21 already shows why the argument’s context matters.

gaps.what: Early theological accounts of the grade of Alexander VII’s judgment
gaps.source: The dispute over the formulary and later theological treatments of dogmatic facts.
gaps.settles: What warrants the attribution of definitive assent to this particular judgment.

cases.next_source: Read the passages in Augustinus bearing on the first four propositions beside the submissions to Rome and the papal acts.

audio.taught: Alexander VII declared that the five condemned propositions really are in Jansen's book and were condemned in the sense he meant. Clement XI added that keeping a respectful silence about this is not enough.
audio.authority: Papal constitutions; a formulary of submission imposed by law. The judgment is what theologians call a dogmatic fact.
audio.permanence: Permanent, on the common view: that the Church can judge which books teach a condemned doctrine. Lapsed: the obligation to sign the formulary.

Checked the Latin of Alexander VII’s declaration and the formulary and of Vineam Domini §6. Compared the judgments with the examples in the 1998 commentary §11 and recorded the open question about the precise grade.
Read Augustinus III.21, cols. 381–382, in the 1640 Louvain edition. Added a comparison of the fifth censure with Jansenius’s discussion of sufficiency and the meaning of all.

evidence_reviews.question: What did the three papal acts require?
evidence_reviews.finding: In 1656 Alexander VII attributed the propositions and the condemned sense to Jansenius. His 1665 formulary made the required submission explicit. In 1705 Clement XI said the faithful owed interior rejection of the condemned sense.
evidence_reviews.test: Use the formulary and Vineam Domini as evidence for the obligation imposed. Compare Augustinus itself with the five propositions to assess how the words express the argument of the book.

evidence_reviews.question: How does the 1998 commentary bear on the grade of the judgment?
evidence_reviews.finding: The commentary illustrates definitive claims connected to revelation by historical necessity. Application to this particular judgment is a theological inference.
evidence_reviews.test: Look for evidence of the intention and mode of the particular act when assessing its grade. Use the earlier bulls to establish what was required of the faithful.

evidence_reviews.question: How does the fifth proposition relate to Jansenius’s argument?
evidence_reviews.finding: Jansenius sets out the sufficient-price reading and then argues that Christ’s offering for someone is directed to that person’s liberation. He reads all as the worldwide Church. This gives a textual basis for comparing his argument with the restricted sense in Innocent X’s censure.
evidence_reviews.test: Read both parts of the chapter. Distinguish the unlimited worth Jansenius reports from his explanation of whom the offering was directed to save. Check the wording of the submitted proposition before judging how closely it follows the book.

cases.title: Unigenitus and the censure of Quesnel
cases.question: What does the bull settle about the 101 propositions, and how far do Augustine and later teaching help us read particular censures?
cases.summary: Clement XI condemns all 101 propositions and applies a list of censures respectively, without assigning a note to each one. The closing clause particularly calls out renewals of propositions of Jansenius in the sense already condemned. The bull separately condemns Quesnel’s book. The Roman preparatory record preserves disagreements that help frame the inquiry into individual propositions. The comparison below tests grace and freedom, grace and the Church, and access to Scripture. Quesnel’s glosses and his 1712 defense help identify what he claims. The final bull gives no individual rationale for propositions 13 and 80.

texts.label: Clement XI, Unigenitus (8 September 1713)
texts.edition: Bullarium Romanum, Turin ed., XXI (1871), pp. 568–575, especially §4, pp. 573–574.
texts.checked: The Latin gives a collective list with respective application. The express sense clause concerns the earlier censures of Jansenius. Section 4 then condemns the book again.

texts.label: Quesnel, Réflexions morales on Luke 5:12–14
texts.edition: Paris, 1698, tome II, pp. 92–93.
texts.checked: The gloss on verse 13 applies Christ’s healing of the leper to absolution through the ministry of the Church.

texts.label: Quesnel, Réflexions morales on Acts 8:27–31
texts.edition: Paris, 1693, tome III, pp. 95–96.
texts.checked: The gloss on verse 28 presents a man occupied with affairs and finances reading Scripture as evidence that the reading is for everyone. The gloss on verse 31 calls it presumptuous to rely on one’s own understanding without the Church’s teachers.

texts.label: Quesnel, Explication apologétique (1712)
texts.edition: First part, pp. 108–113, especially pp. 112–113.
texts.checked: Quesnel includes the line about the touch of grace in his defense of absolutely efficacious grace. He distinguishes the immediate effect God absolutely wills from a further effect that may be resisted.

texts.label: Augustine, De correptione et gratia
texts.edition: De correptione et gratia 14.43 (PL 44, col. 942).
texts.checked: Augustine says that no human will resists God when he wills to save, in a discussion of the efficacy of divine action and of correction.

texts.label: Vatican II, Lumen Gentium §16
texts.edition: Vatican English edition, 21 November 1964.
texts.checked: Section 16 speaks of grace among those without knowledge of the Gospel and of their relation to the people of God.

texts.label: Pius VI, Auctorem fidei, proposition 67
texts.edition: Vatican Italian edition, 28 August 1794, proposition 67. Denzinger Latin at DS 2667.
texts.checked: Pius VI censures the Pistoian doctrine that only true inability excuses failure to read Scripture, with its claim about the effects of neglect. He identifies this doctrine as previously condemned in Quesnel.

texts.label: Vatican II, Dei Verbum §§22, 25
texts.edition: Vatican English edition, 18 November 1965.
texts.checked: Section 22 calls for easy access to Scripture for all the faithful. Section 25 urges them to read frequently and asks bishops to provide suitable instruction and editions.

propositions.says: Proposition 13 says that when God wills to save a soul and touches it with interior grace, no human will resists him.
propositions.note: On Luke 5:13, Quesnel compares the healing of the leper to Christ healing sinners through the Church’s ministry. He invokes efficacious grace when defending this language in 1712. Gres-Gayer reports a preliminary suspension of judgment.

propositions.says: Quesnel says that a grace achieves the immediate effect God absolutely intends, while its further effect may be resisted. He identifies the touch of grace as an example of absolutely efficacious grace.
propositions.note: He says that the person retains the power to reject grace. His defense appeals to Thomist authors and expressly rejects the second Jansenist proposition.

propositions.says: When God wills to save, no human will resists him.
The will moved by God can dissent if it wishes and cooperates by assenting to his call.
Clement XI condemns every proposition under a list of censures applied respectively, singling out renewals of condemned Jansenist propositions in their condemned sense.
Proposition 29 says that outside the Church no grace is granted.
propositions.note: See B3 for how the Church’s role in salvation bears on this proposition.

propositions.says: God’s grace can act among people who have yet to receive the Gospel and can move them to seek God and do his will.
Proposition 79 calls study of Scripture useful and necessary at all times, in all places, and for every kind of person.
Proposition 80 says that the reading of Sacred Scripture is for all.
propositions.note: In the gloss on Acts 8:31 Quesnel requires the help of the Church’s teachers to understand Scripture.

propositions.says: The council calls for easy access to Scripture for all the Christian faithful, urges them to read frequently, and directs bishops to teach them how to use it well.

matrix.why: The words closely parallel Augustine. The gloss applies the claim to healing through the Church’s ministry. Quesnel’s defense calls it a case of absolutely efficacious grace. The final bull gives no individual note or rationale.

Trent affirms the power to dissent when God moves the will. Quesnel also affirms that power in his defense and allows that grace can be resisted with respect to its further effect. His additional claim that an immediate effect absolutely willed by God always occurs requires its own comparison with Trent and Cum occasione.

Grace can reach people outside visible Catholic communion. This later teaching accords with the rejection of a blanket denial of grace beyond the Church’s visible bounds. Lumen Gentium still speaks of these people’s relation to the people of God.

The council urges frequent reading with instruction and pastoral provision. Proposition 79 asserts necessity at all times and places for every kind of person. Pius VI connects a Pistoian doctrine of obligation with what had already been condemned in Quesnel.

Quesnel takes the Ethiopian’s reading as a model for everyone. In the same passage he insists on help from the Church’s teachers. This gives real overlap with Dei Verbum §25. Establishing a further implication in proposition 80 or the reason for its censure requires more evidence.

cases.qualifications: Omnes et singulas covers every listed proposition. Respective applies the list of censures without naming an individual grade. In eo sensu, in quo hae damnatae fuerunt refers to the earlier censures of Jansenius’s propositions.
cases.reception: French opponents appealed to a future council. Gres-Gayer reports that Fénelon urged individual censures during drafting. In Auctorem fidei 67, Pius VI identifies the Pistoian doctrine on the obligation to read Scripture as previously condemned in Quesnel. He gives no Unigenitus proposition number.
cases.contingency: Section 4 also prescribes penalties for defending the propositions or circulating the book. The legal enforcement history is a separate question from the sense and grade of an individual doctrinal censure.
cases.development: Lumen Gentium §16 describes grace at work among people who have not heard the Gospel. Dei Verbum §§22 and 25 call for easy access to Scripture and invite all the faithful to read it with prayer and pastoral guidance. Proposition 80 remains the closest comparison on Scripture.
cases.hypothesis: Quesnel’s defense offers a possible account of the scope of proposition 13. The glosses on Acts show that Quesnel both commends broad reading and insists on ecclesial instruction. Each comparison must still account for the wording of the operative censure and the evidence about its rationale. (T)
cases.objection: Proposition 13 echoes Augustine closely. Proposition 80 appears to say what Vatican II later urges. What evidence shows which sense or implication drew either censure?
cases.rebuttal: The Roman record supports a Catholic reading of proposition 13 as a live possibility at the preliminary stage. Quesnel’s defense explains why he thought his account differed from a denial of the power of resistance. His proposition was still censured. The force of “necessary” in proposition 79 explains its distance from Dei Verbum §25. For proposition 80, the original gloss explicitly values ecclesial teaching. The precise ground for the censure remains open.

gaps.what: The grounds for the censures on propositions 13 and 80
gaps.source: Ceyssens’s edition of the Roman judgments and votes, contemporary episcopal explanations, and earlier French editions of the glosses.
gaps.settles: Which implications were objected to and whether any contemporary source accounts for the overlap with Augustine or later teaching on Scripture.

gaps.what: Quesnel’s theory of sufficient grace
gaps.source: The rest of the Explication apologétique, the glosses underlying propositions 9–16, and Roman examinations of those passages.
gaps.settles: Whether his distinction between immediate and final effects preserves the ability to dissent in the sense affirmed by Trent.

cases.next_source: Locate the votes on propositions 13 and 80 and compare them with Quesnel’s account of the two passages and his defense of sufficient grace.

audio.taught: Clement the Eleventh condemned all one hundred and one propositions of Quesnel and also condemned his book.
audio.authority: The papal constitution names a list of censures applied respectively. It gives no individual grade for proposition thirteen or proposition eighty.
audio.permanence: The censure stands. The meaning and grounds of individual censures remain questions for the original text and its reception.

evidence_reviews.question: What does the Latin say about the sense condemned?
evidence_reviews.finding: Section 4 names every proposition and uses respective. It singles out renewals of Jansenius’s propositions in the sense in which those earlier propositions were condemned. It then condemns the book as a whole.
evidence_reviews.test: Use the express sense clause for the connection to Jansenius. Establish any further contextual qualification from the proposition and the evidence about its use.

evidence_reviews.question: Does proposition 13 condemn Augustine’s teaching on efficacious grace?
evidence_reviews.finding: Quesnel applies the healing of the leper to the Church’s ministry. In 1712 he invoked absolutely efficacious grace and stated that a grace may be resisted as to its further effect. Gres-Gayer reports Clement’s preliminary suspension of judgment. The proposition was included in the final list.
evidence_reviews.test: Compare Quesnel’s own account of sufficient grace with Trent and the second Jansenist proposition. Use the Roman votes to assess what drew censure. Quesnel’s defense records his position in the controversy.

evidence_reviews.question: What does proposition 29 clarify about grace and the Church?
evidence_reviews.finding: Lumen Gentium §16 speaks both of grace reaching people who have yet to hear the Gospel and of their relation to God’s people.
evidence_reviews.test: Distinguish absence of visible communion from separation in every sense when comparing the two texts.

evidence_reviews.question: Does the censure of propositions 79 and 80 conflict with Vatican II on Scripture?
evidence_reviews.finding: Proposition 79 asserts an unrestricted necessity. The gloss behind proposition 80 commends reading even among those occupied with public affairs. The comment on Acts 8:31 calls for the help of the Church’s teachers. Dei Verbum §25 also joins wide access to pastoral instruction.
evidence_reviews.test: Auctorem fidei 67 confirms that an obligation with virtually no exceptions was at issue in the reception of Quesnel. It gives no Unigenitus proposition number. Check the Roman and early reception evidence for the specific objection to proposition 80.

research_sources.title: J. M. Gres-Gayer, The Unigenitus of Clement XI
research_sources.citation: Theological Studies 49 (1988), pp. 259–282, especially pp. 267–270.
research_sources.note: The study reports Clement’s preliminary suspension on proposition 13, the discussions of other selected propositions, and the collective censure of the final bull.

cases.title: Pistoia on liturgical language and Scripture reading
cases.question: What exactly did Pius VI censure about the vernacular and Scripture reading, and how do those judgments compare with Vatican II?
cases.summary: Pistoia proposed a diocesan manual with both Latin and vernacular texts. In proposition 66, Pius VI censured the charge of acting against apostolic practice and God’s designs insofar as it referred to introducing the vernacular into liturgical prayers. Trent and Vatican II both allow for instruction and participation. Vatican II allows the competent authority to extend vernacular use. In proposition 67, Pius VI censured Pistoia’s claim that only genuine inability excuses a person from reading Scripture, together with its account of the effects of neglect. The original synod places that claim in a note to a qualified statement.

texts.label: Synod of Pistoia, Atti e decreti (1786)
texts.edition: Pistoia, Atto Bracali, session III, p. 100, article 11 and its note. Session VI, Della preghiera §24, p. 206.
texts.checked: The main text calls Scripture reading useful and denies that everyone needs it for salvation. The note says only genuine inability excuses omission. The proposal on public prayer calls for a bilingual ritual and manual.

texts.label: Pius VI, Auctorem fidei (28 August 1794)
texts.edition: Typographia Reverendae Camerae Apostolicae, Latin printing, propositions 31–35 and 66–67.
texts.checked: The bull gives individual censures. Proposition 66 includes the condition about introducing the vernacular into liturgical prayers. Proposition 67 cites Quesnel without naming a numbered article.

texts.label: Trent, session XXII, chapter 8 and canon 9 (1562)
texts.edition: J. Waterworth, 1848 English edition. Denzinger Latin for chapter 8 and canon 9.
texts.checked: The chapter declines vernacular celebration everywhere and orders explanation to the people. Canon 9 censures the claim that the Mass must be celebrated only in the vernacular.

texts.label: Vatican II, Sacrosanctum Concilium §§36, 54 (1963)
texts.edition: Vatican English edition, 4 December 1963.
texts.checked: Section 36 preserves Latin in the Latin rites subject to particular law and regulates the extension of the vernacular. Section 54 applies the regulation to Mass and provides for the faithful to say or sing their parts in Latin.

texts.label: Vatican II, Dei Verbum §§22, 25 (1965)
texts.edition: Vatican English edition, 18 November 1965.
texts.checked: The constitution asks for easy access to Scripture, urges frequent reading and assigns bishops a role in instruction and suitable translations.

propositions.says: The synod says that failing to provide easier ways of joining the people’s voice to the Church’s prayer would offend apostolic practice and God’s designs. It proposes a bilingual ritual and manual.
Pius VI censures the claim insofar as it is understood of introducing the vernacular into liturgical prayers.
Trent censures the claim that Mass must be celebrated only in the vernacular.
Vatican II retains Latin in the Latin rites and provides for wider use of the vernacular under competent authority.

Pistoia calls reading Scripture useful and denies that every individual needs it to attain salvation. The attached note says that only genuine inability excuses omission and blames neglect for obscuring basic truths.
propositions.ext: Pistoia, session III, article 11 and its note

propositions.says: Pius VI censures the rule in the note and its claim about neglect, calling the doctrine previously condemned in Quesnel.
Vatican II urges frequent Scripture reading by all the faithful and provides for ecclesial instruction and access.

matrix.why: The synod grounds easier participation in an appeal to apostolic practice and proposes a manual with both languages. The censure expressly targets the sense involving the introduction of vernacular into liturgical prayers. The local implementation would help fix the reach of that sense.
Pius VI judges a proposition about the introduction of vernacular prayers as a requirement of apostolic practice and God’s designs. Vatican II gives competent authority a regulated permission.
Trent rejects an exclusive obligation to use the vernacular. Vatican II retains Latin while allowing wider vernacular use under regulation.
The censure names an obligation excused only by genuine inability, along with an account of its neglect. Vatican II urges reading and asks the Church’s ministers to facilitate it.

cases.qualifications: The bull’s introduction calls for propositions to be censured individually and sometimes in their connection with others. The term intellecta introduces a condition in proposition 66. In proposition 67 Pius VI identifies a specific note to the decree on grace. His reference to Quesnel gives no individual Unigenitus grade.
cases.reception: Vatican II put regulated vernacular use into its own liturgical constitution. The practical extent of permitted use was later developed through the authorized revisions of the liturgical books.
cases.contingency: Languages and authorized forms of celebration fall within liturgical regulation. The censure also addresses the claim of apostolic and divine necessity, which requires a separate judgment.
cases.development: The conciliar texts preserve the aim of instructing the faithful and enabling their participation. Dei Verbum calls for Scripture access and reading together with pastoral assistance.
cases.hypothesis: A comparison of obligations, permissions and historical judgments explains why Vatican II can endorse some practical aims associated with Pistoia. Each censure needs to be read with its own condition and object. (T)
cases.objection: Pistoia already wanted a bilingual text and a guided reading of Scripture. Does a later ecclesial preference for these things show that Pius VI had condemned that same policy?
cases.rebuttal: The actual synod and bull identify more specific claims. The first combines a local policy with an appeal about what apostolic practice demands, and Pius VI adds an express condition. The second adds a general obligation in a note to a more limited claim about salvation. The conciliar permissions and exhortations can be compared against those precise claims.

gaps.what: How Pistoia intended its bilingual books to be used in public worship
gaps.source: Ricci’s rubrics and pastoral instructions and evidence of diocesan implementation after 1786.
gaps.settles: Whether the books were meant to change the language actually spoken in particular liturgical acts or chiefly to help people follow them.

gaps.what: The full range of Pistoian liturgical and penitential proposals
gaps.source: The Eucharist and Penance decrees behind Auctorem fidei 31–35, with their publication and application.
gaps.settles: Whether the comparisons made here also explain those distinct censures.

cases.next_source: Read the rubrics or drafts of Pistoia’s planned ritual and manual beside Della preghiera §24 and Pius VI’s condition.

audio.taught: Pistoia proposed a bilingual manual. Pius the Sixth censured a specified reading of its proposal and a separate claim about the obligation to read Scripture.
audio.authority: The bull names individual censures. Vatican Two addresses the authority to regulate liturgical language and encourages frequent reading of Scripture.
audio.permanence: The comparison turns on the scope of a necessity, a permission, and an exhortation. The proposed diocesan practice requires more evidence.

Checked the acts of Pistoia, the Roman Latin of propositions 31–35 and 66–67, and Trent and Vatican II. Distinguished the local bilingual proposal and the note on the obligation to read Scripture.

evidence_reviews.question: What did Pistoia actually propose in §24?
evidence_reviews.finding: The synod proposed that a bishop oversee a bilingual ritual and manual with explanations, including ordinary Mass texts and rites of the sacraments. Its reason invokes apostolic practice and God’s designs.
evidence_reviews.test: Compare the proposal’s details with the express condition in proposition 66. Consult rubrics before equating the proposed use of the book with the language of the celebrant.

evidence_reviews.question: Does Vatican II prescribe the proposition censured by Pius VI?
evidence_reviews.finding: Trent rejects the exclusive necessity of the vernacular. Vatican II provides for Latin and regulates when the vernacular may be extended.
evidence_reviews.test: Test the claim of necessity and the act granting permission in their own terms, including the competent authority.

evidence_reviews.question: What does the note on Scripture add to Pistoia’s main text?
evidence_reviews.finding: Article 11 denies that reading is necessary for every individual to be saved and insists on deference to Church authority. Its note makes only true inability an excuse from reading and ascribes doctrinal obscurity to neglect.
evidence_reviews.test: Compare that note with Auctorem fidei 67, Quesnel’s propositions 79 and 80, and Dei Verbum. A censure of the note does not by itself assign a grade or rationale to Quesnel’s proposition 80.

cases.title: Baius on concupiscence and the gratuity of grace
cases.question: What do Trent and the condemnation of Baius establish about remaining concupiscence and the gratuity of the supernatural order?
cases.summary: Trent says that baptism remits the guilt of original sin. Remaining concupiscence comes from sin and inclines to it, and does no harm to people who withhold consent and resist with grace. Pius V censures 79 propositions respectively. Proposition 75 calls the felt impulse a breach of the commandment while withholding imputation as sin. Propositions 21, 24 and 26 raise a different question about what nature is owed. The scope of the concession in the censure clause depends on the disputed punctuation called the Comma Pianum.

texts.label: Trent, session V, decree on original sin (17 June 1546)
texts.edition: Decree on Original Sin, canon 5. J. Waterworth, 1848 English edition, and the Denzinger Latin at DS 1515.
texts.checked: The decree distinguishes the guilt remitted in baptism from concupiscence that remains, and names non-consent and resistance by grace.

texts.label: Pius V, Ex omnibus afflictionibus (1 October 1567)
texts.edition: Bullarium Romanum, Turin ed., VIII (1863), Pius V’s bull as inserted in Provisionis nostrae, especially p. 319.
texts.checked: The printed witness places a comma after possent, unlike the site’s Denzinger Latin. Its proposition 75 also lacks the explicit “and does not consent” found in Denzinger.

texts.label: Gregory XIII, Provisionis nostrae (1580)
texts.edition: Bullarium Romanum, Turin ed., VIII (1863), pp. 314–320. The Roman text dates the constitution January 1579 by the Incarnation year.
texts.checked: Gregory confirms Pius V’s letters, inserts their text, and orders that the inserted tenor carry the same evidentiary force as the earlier letters.

texts.label: Pius XII, Humani generis §26 (1950)
texts.edition: Vatican English edition, §26.
texts.checked: Pius XII defends the gratuity of the supernatural order against the claim that God cannot create intellectual beings without ordering and calling them to the beatific vision.

propositions.quote: the whole of that which has the true and proper nature of sin is not taken away
propositions.says: Trent says baptism removes original guilt. Concupiscence remains, comes from sin, and inclines to sin. It is not properly sin in the reborn and cannot harm those who withhold consent and resist with Christ’s grace.
Proposition 74 calls concupiscence itself sin in the baptized who have relapsed into mortal sin and in whom it dominates, comparing it to vicious habits.
propositions.note: The Latin in quibus refers back to the baptized who have relapsed.

propositions.says: Proposition 75 calls the felt impulse a breach of “Thou shalt not covet,” although the breach is not reckoned as sin.
propositions.note: The Denzinger witness explicitly adds that the person does not consent. The Turin text goes directly from feeling the impulse to transgressing the commandment.

propositions.says: Pius V condemns the propositions respectively under a list of censures. The clause refers both to possible ways of defending some propositions and to their proper and strict sense as intended by their proponents.
propositions.note: The Denzinger English takes the latter phrase with the censure. The placement of the comma is historically disputed.

propositions.says: Proposition 21 makes participation in divine nature due to original integrity and calls it natural.
Proposition 24 calls it Pelagian to say that gifts superadded to nature raised humanity to adoptive sonship.
Proposition 26 calls original integrity the natural condition of humanity and denies that this integrity was an undeserved elevation.
Pius XII rejects the thesis that God cannot create intellectual beings without ordering and calling them to the beatific vision.

matrix.why: Trent says concupiscence cannot harm the baptized who withhold consent and resist by grace. Proposition 75 predicates transgression of the felt impulse, while expressly withholding imputation as sin. There would be a conflict if that transgression meant a culpable violation by the person.

Proposition 74 concerns people in mortal sin. The comparison turns on whether it attributes sin to the inclination itself or is speaking of a habit formed or sustained by voluntary acts. The text expressly calls concupiscence sin in that setting.

Both acts bear on the gratuity of supernatural elevation. The bull censures a proposition that makes participation in divine nature due to original integrity. Humani generis rejects a claim about what God must give any intellect he creates.

cases.qualifications: Respective assigns a range of censures to the list without naming the grade of any numbered proposition. The disputed phrase in rigore et proprio verborum sensu ab assertoribus intento can be attached to the censure or to the preceding concession, depending on punctuation.
cases.reception: Gregory XIII confirmed and reissued Pius V’s text in Provisionis nostrae. The punctuation dispute persisted. Later debate about the natural desire for God raised a distinct question about the meaning of an elevation being due to nature.
cases.contingency: The act’s doctrinal censures and its disciplinary restrictions on disputation carry different kinds of force.
cases.development: The Catechism §1264 repeats Trent’s teaching that concupiscence cannot harm those who resist it by grace. Humani generis §26 specifies a limit for theology of the supernatural order by rejecting any requirement that God call every intellectual creature to the beatific vision.
cases.hypothesis: The distinction between inclination and culpable consent clarifies the relation to Trent. The distinction between a natural desire and a claim of entitlement clarifies the relation to later theology of grace. Which censures apply to specific propositions and which words the concession governs require separate evidence. (T)
cases.objection: If proposition 75 denies imputation as sin, what exactly drew censure? If the human intellect naturally desires God, does that desire make supernatural elevation due?
cases.rebuttal: The site can identify the question raised by calling involuntary experience a transgression. The individual censure remains unstated. A desire for God and an obligation on God are distinct claims. The named propositions and Humani generis give evidence for assessing the second claim. The first requires a further theological argument.

gaps.what: Early textual witnesses to Ex omnibus and the scope of the concession
gaps.source: Contemporary copies of the 1567 bull, Denzinger’s source and apparatus, and the Louvain and Roman transmission of the text.
gaps.settles: The authority of the competing punctuation and wording, including the non-consent line in proposition 75.

gaps.what: The grounds for individual censures on concupiscence and original integrity
gaps.source: Baius’s original treatises, the propositions submitted to Rome, and contemporary accounts of examination and reception.
gaps.settles: Whether individual propositions are judged for a claim of culpability, a claim about what is due to nature, or another implication.

cases.next_source: Compare the 1567 witnesses and Baius’s treatises with the Gregorian reissue and the Denzinger apparatus for propositions 74 and 75 and the closing clause.

audio.taught: Trent says baptism remits original sin while concupiscence remains. Pius the Fifth censured propositions of Baius on concupiscence, original integrity, and grace.
audio.authority: The bull applies censures respectively. Its concession about the possible defense of some propositions is subject to a dispute about punctuation.
audio.permanence: Trent’s teaching and the gratuity of the supernatural order give limits for comparison. The grades of particular censures and the full account of natural desire require further evidence.
