Compared Trent’s canon, Pius V’s Latin as printed in the Gregorian reissue, and the Denzinger witness. Added the comparison with Humani generis §26 on gratuity.

evidence_reviews.question: What does the Comma Pianum change?
evidence_reviews.finding: The Gregorian reissue as printed in the Turin Bullarium puts a comma after possent. On the reading reflected by the Denzinger English, the strict sense specifies the condemnation. On the other attachment, it qualifies the concession about what some propositions might sustain.
evidence_reviews.test: Compare earlier textual witnesses and their reception. Neither attachment gives the individual note for any one proposition.

evidence_reviews.question: Do propositions 74 and 75 predicate the same thing as Trent?
evidence_reviews.finding: Trent speaks of the inclination persisting in the baptized. Proposition 74 specifies relapse and domination. Proposition 75 calls the felt impulse a transgression while saying that it is not imputed as sin. The Denzinger Latin explicitly adds non-consent.
evidence_reviews.test: Check whether Baius understands transgression as culpable consent, involuntary disorder, or another kind of breach. Keep the subjects of each proposition distinct.

evidence_reviews.question: Which claims about nature and grace are actually at issue?
evidence_reviews.finding: Proposition 21 calls participation in divine nature due to original integrity. Propositions 24 and 26 challenge the language of superadded gift and undeserved elevation. Pius XII rejects the necessity of a supernatural call for any creature with intellect.
evidence_reviews.test: Ask whether a proposed account of natural desire entails that God owes the supernatural end. Assess that implication before comparing the account with Baius.

research_sources.title: E. Boissard, Note sur le sens « propre et rigoureux » de certaines propositions de Baius
research_sources.citation: Revue des sciences religieuses 36 (1962), pp. 140–153.
research_sources.note: Boissard examines how a censure can stand even if a proposition once had a defensible proper sense in a different linguistic or theological setting.

cases.title: Quierzy and Valence on predestination and redemption
cases.question: Can the two local councils’ accounts of Christ’s death be read together, and what limits do Trent and Cum occasione set?
cases.summary: Quierzy says Christ suffered for every human being and illustrates universal sufficiency with a remedy that helps only when taken. Valence rejects applying the shedding of Christ’s blood to the already damned and speaks of the price given for believers. It also rejects four chapters identified with Quierzy. A distinction between the scope of the passion and its saving application fits Trent and explains some of the language. Whether it fully accounts for Valence’s restriction and explicit rejection of the four chapters remains open.

texts.label: Local council of Quierzy (853), four chapters
texts.edition: Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Concilia 3, ed. W. Hartmann (1984), p. 297, chapters 1–4.
texts.checked: Chapter 4 asserts universal suffering, distinguishes who is redeemed by the mystery of the passion, and uses the image of a remedy able to benefit everyone.

texts.label: Local council of Valence (855), canons 3–5
texts.edition: Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Concilia 3, ed. W. Hartmann (1984), pp. 353–356, especially p. 355, note 27.
texts.checked: Canon 4 rejects the shedding of Christ’s blood for those already eternally damned and treats the price in connection with believers. It rejects four earlier chapters as well as a separate set of nineteen syllogisms. Canon 5 affirms genuine redemption in baptism even for some who later fail to persevere.

texts.label: Council of Trent, decree on justification (1547)
texts.edition: Session VI, chapters 3 and 15 and canon 17. J. Waterworth, 1848 English edition, with the Denzinger Latin.
texts.checked: Christ died for all. The benefit is communicated to some. Trent rejects limiting justificatory grace to the predestined and teaches that true justification can be lost.

texts.label: Innocent X, Cum occasione (31 May 1653)
texts.edition: Bullarium Romanum, Turin ed., XV (1868), pp. 720–722, especially §4 at p. 721.
texts.checked: Checked all five censures in Latin. In the fifth, dumtaxat limits the heretical sense to the claim that Christ died for the salvation of the predestined alone.

propositions.says: God predestines the elect to life. He foreknows the loss of the others and predestines their just punishment without predestining them to perish by sin.
God wills all human beings without exception to be saved, though not all are saved.
Christ suffered for every human being. The remedy can benefit all, but its saving effect requires receiving it.
Valence speaks of predestination to life and death. It reserves predestination to what God himself does in mercy or judgment, and excludes human malice from what he predestines.
Valence rejects saying the blood was shed even for the already damned before the passion. It refers the payment of the price to those described as believing.
propositions.note: Canon 4 also rejects the four earlier chapters. Its identification with Quierzy is given in the critical edition’s notes.

propositions.says: Valence says that those truly regenerated in baptism are truly redeemed and washed of sins. Some fail to persevere and do not attain final salvation.
Christ died for all, and only those to whom the merits of his passion are communicated receive the benefit of his death.
Innocent X rejects the charge of Semipelagianism. The additional note of heresy applies in the specified sense that Christ died for the salvation of the predestined alone.

matrix.why: Quierzy numbers predestination as one and distinguishes grace and punishment. Valence speaks of two outcomes while restricting divine predestination to God’s own acts of mercy and justice. Both deny that God predestines human malice.

The contrast between universal suffering and particular saving application could account for the wording. Valence expressly contests earlier chapters and excludes the already damned from the scope of the assertion it rejects. The sense of that exclusion has to be established from its own context.
Both distinguish dying for all from all sharing in saving benefit. Quierzy’s remedy image explicitly affirms universal capacity to benefit.

Valence treats people who subsequently fail to persevere as genuinely redeemed through baptism. That distinction gives direct evidence against treating its believers as identical with the finally predestined.

cases.qualifications: The ninth-century witnesses are local synods. Quierzy distinguishes Christ’s suffering from being redeemed by the mystery of his passion. Valence’s term for the price and its exclusion of the already damned require attention to the specific controversy.
cases.reception: Valence’s canon 4 sets itself against four chapters attributed to Quierzy. The later efforts at Langres and Savonnières are relevant to what was retained or reconciled.
cases.contingency: The local prohibitions, the vocabulary of the dispute, and the doctrinal claims about the passion and its fruits require separate judgments.
cases.development: Trent expressly combines universal death with particular reception of the benefit. The later censure in Cum occasione sets a limit on restricting the saving scope of Christ’s death to the predestined alone.
cases.hypothesis: Christ’s death has a genuinely universal saving sufficiency, while saving benefits must be communicated and can be lost. This accounts for Quierzy, Trent and Valence’s teaching on baptism. Its adequacy to the exact exclusion in Valence 4 remains to be tested. (T)
cases.objection: Valence does not simply describe people who fail to receive a benefit. It contests the claim about blood shed for those already damned. Why should its words be taken as a restriction on application?
cases.rebuttal: Valence’s reference to believers and its next canon on people truly redeemed without final perseverance provide grounds for reading it in terms of the communication of redemption. Its explicit objection in canon 4 still requires an explanation from the debate and from the subsequent negotiations.

gaps.what: The specific thesis targeted by Valence’s example of the already damned
gaps.source: The texts of Hincmar, Florus, and the Lorraine and Lyon responses surrounding the two councils.
gaps.settles: Whether the excluded claim concerns intention, payment of the price, or application of the effects of the passion.

gaps.what: The reception of the contested chapters after 855
gaps.source: The Latin acts and surrounding correspondence for Langres and Savonnières (859) in the MGH.
gaps.settles: Which formulas were revised, dropped or received during attempts at agreement.

cases.next_source: Trace the discussion of the already damned in the Lyon responses and later conference documents.

audio.taught: Quierzy says Christ suffered for all and uses the image of a remedy. Valence distinguishes those who are truly redeemed from those who persevere.
audio.authority: The earlier witnesses are local councils. Trent distinguishes Christ dying for all from people receiving the benefit, and Innocent the Tenth censures a specified restriction.
audio.permanence: The universal death and the particular reception of grace can stand together. The exact objection made by Valence still needs an explanation.

evidence_reviews.question: Do Quierzy and Valence teach opposite causes of damnation?
evidence_reviews.finding: Both place malice on the human side and punishment within divine judgment. Their ways of counting predestination differ.
evidence_reviews.test: Test whether their differing use of predestination changes the thing predestined, especially the difference between sinful action and its punishment.

evidence_reviews.question: How strong is Quierzy’s statement of sufficiency?
evidence_reviews.finding: It says Christ suffered for everyone and that the remedy has in itself the capacity to benefit all. It gives unbelief and lack of faith working through love as the reason that not all are healed.
evidence_reviews.test: Distinguish universal ability to benefit from a theory about the intentions of God or the distribution of every particular aid.

evidence_reviews.question: What makes Valence the hard case?
evidence_reviews.finding: Canon 4 rejects four earlier chapters and has narrower language about the price. Canon 5 affirms actual redemption in some who do not attain eternal salvation.
evidence_reviews.test: Find the use of blood shed for the already damned in the arguments Valence answers. The explicit rejection carries more evidentiary weight than a reconciliation based on vocabulary alone.

log.change: Compared Quierzy and Valence against the MGH Latin and checked Trent and the fifth Jansenist censure. Kept Valence’s explicit rejection as an unresolved point.

cases.title: De auxiliis and the power to resist grace
cases.question: How do Báñez, Molina and Quesnel account for free consent under grace, and what did Rome actually settle?
cases.summary: Trent teaches that prevenient grace moves the will, which truly cooperates and can dissent. Báñez and Molina differ on what explains the efficacy of an aid that produces consent. Báñez distinguishes an invitation that can be refused from grace that infallibly brings about free consent by divine motion. Molina says people can respond differently to equal aids and uses middle knowledge to explain the certainty of foreknowledge. Quesnel allows resistance to a further effect but says the immediate effect God absolutely wills always occurs. The Roman acts leave the schools’ dispute open, and the comparison with Quesnel turns on the substance of the power to dissent.

texts.label: Council of Trent, decree on justification (1547)
texts.edition: Session VI, chapter 5 and canons 4–5. J. Waterworth, 1848 English edition, and the Denzinger Latin.
texts.checked: The decree names prevenient grace, the person’s actual cooperation, the possibility of dissent, and the persistence of free will after the fall.

texts.label: Luis de Molina, Concordia
texts.edition: Paris, P. Lethielleux, 1876, on I q. 14 a. 13, disputations 12 and 52, and on I q. 23 aa. 4–5, disputation 1, member 6, pp. 462–463.
texts.checked: Molina says equal interior aids can receive different responses. His middle knowledge concerns what a free agent would do while retaining the capacity to do otherwise. He distinguishes a person’s cooperation from the supernatural efficacy that comes from grace.

texts.label: Domingo Báñez, Disputatio and Responsio on the efficacy of grace
texts.edition: Latin transcription of the exchange with Jesuit theologians, ca. 1599–1600. Disputatio §§11, 34–35 and Responsio answers 1–5. The edition identifies Biblioteca Angelica, cod. 862 for the Responsio.
texts.checked: Báñez distinguishes the aids that invite and can be refused from divine aid that brings about consent infallibly. He attributes the act of consent to the will as a real, subordinate cause.

texts.label: Paul V on the Congregatio de Auxiliis (1607)
texts.edition: Denzinger, n. 1090 (DS 1997), from the formula sent to both superiors on 5 September 1607.
texts.checked: The printed formula sends the disputants home and forbids either side to censure the other. It anticipates a later determination. Independent review of the source behind the printed formula remains open.

texts.label: Innocent X, Cum occasione (31 May 1653)
texts.edition: Bullarium Romanum, Turin ed., XV (1868), pp. 720–722, especially §4 at p. 721.
texts.checked: Checked all five censures in Latin. In the fifth, dumtaxat limits the heretical sense to the claim that Christ died for the salvation of the predestined alone.

texts.label: Innocent X, decree on alleged acts of De auxiliis (23 April 1654)
texts.edition: Denzinger, n. 1097 (DS 2008), referring to Paul V and Urban VIII.
texts.checked: The decree printed in Denzinger disallows an alleged constitution condemning Molina and directs the parties to observe the decrees of Paul V and Urban VIII.

texts.label: Quesnel, Explication apologétique (1712)
texts.edition: First part, pp. 108–113, especially pp. 112–113.
texts.checked: Quesnel includes the line about the touch of grace in his defense of absolutely efficacious grace. He distinguishes the immediate effect God absolutely wills from a further effect that may be resisted.

texts.label: Clement XI, Unigenitus (8 September 1713)
texts.edition: Bullarium Romanum, Turin ed., XXI (1871), pp. 568–575, especially §4, pp. 573–574.
texts.checked: The Latin gives a collective list with respective application. The express sense clause concerns the earlier censures of Jansenius. Section 4 then condemns the book again.

propositions.says: The will moved and aroused by God can dissent if it wills and actively cooperates when it assents.
For Molina, equal interior aids can meet different responses. God knows what the person would freely do in given circumstances, and the supernatural character of the salutary act comes from grace.
propositions.ext: Molina, Concordia, disputations 12 and 52, and q. 23 aa. 4–5

propositions.says: Báñez distinguishes an inviting aid that can be refused from properly efficacious aid, with which actual dissent cannot coexist. The will itself actively and freely consents under divine motion.
Paul V ends the proceedings and prohibits each side from censuring the other while reserving a decision.
Innocent X declares heretical the proposition that in fallen nature one never resists interior grace.
Innocent X disallows alleged acts circulated in support of either party and an alleged constitution of Paul V condemning Molina.
Quesnel says a person retains the power to resist. He says the immediate effect absolutely willed by God occurs, while a further effect may be hindered.
propositions.note: Quesnel appeals to Thomist authors. His defense is evidence for his own position. His proposition 13 still appears in the final Unigenitus list.

matrix.why: Molina reads Trent as teaching the power to refuse interior grace, and expressly distinguishes grace as necessary for a salutary act from free consent under grace.

Báñez allows an inviting interior aid to be refused. He denies the coexistence of actual dissent with the aid that infallibly brings about consent. The disputed question is whether his account preserves the power of the will, under grace, in the sense affirmed by Trent.

The authors give opposed answers about the cause of efficacy. For Báñez an efficacious aid, as given by God, infallibly produces free consent. Molina makes free cooperation a condition for the aid to be efficacious with respect to the resulting act. Both require grace and an active will.
The censure concerns never resisting interior grace. Báñez explicitly allows refusal of interior invitation and restricts the incompatibility with actual dissent to efficacious aid.

Quesnel explicitly rejects the universal denial of resistance. His claim that every grace secures the immediately intended effect leaves a further question about what the person has real power to refuse and how his account bears on the censured proposition.

Paul V forbids the parties to censure each other. Innocent X refuses evidentiary weight to circulating texts, including the alleged condemnation of Molina, and directs the parties to observe the earlier decrees.

cases.qualifications: Separate the cause of a grace’s efficacy, the power to dissent, and the fact that dissent does or does not occur. In particular, the proposition censured by Innocent X uses the quantifier never.
cases.reception: Paul V leaves a declaration for a later time and forbids partisan censures. In 1654 Innocent X disallows alleged records and a supposed constitution condemning Molina. This identifies which documentary claims cannot decide the dispute.
cases.contingency: The directions about how the schools conduct their dispute are juridical. The doctrinal comparison rests on Trent’s teaching and the text of the Jansenist censure.
cases.development: The distinction between inviting grace and grace that effects consent helps compare the schools with later censures. The causes and conditions of efficacy still admit competing theological accounts.
cases.hypothesis: The ability to dissent needs a positive explanation in each account. An assertion about the actual consent produced by a specified efficacious aid can have a different scope from denying that any interior aid can ever be refused. (T)
cases.objection: If consent infallibly follows the efficacious aid, how can the will dissent if it wills in the precise sense of Trent? Calling a different aid resistible leaves the modal question about the person under precisely this aid.
cases.rebuttal: Báñez expressly treats consent as the will’s own act and locates the efficacy that secures it in God. Molina distinguishes the certainty of what God knows from necessity in the free act. Those are positive accounts with a real difference. Quesnel’s separate argument still has to meet the same test, including what his sufficient aid makes possible.

gaps.what: The power to dissent under properly efficacious aid
gaps.source: Báñez’s related treatments of concurrence and the later scholastic discussion of the power considered apart from and in conjunction with the actual divine motion.
gaps.settles: Whether each account gives a coherent reading of the same power affirmed in Trent.

gaps.what: Quesnel’s account of sufficient grace beyond his defense of the gloss
gaps.source: The rest of the 1712 Explication apologétique, his related propositions and the Roman votes for Unigenitus.
gaps.settles: Whether the power he attributes to grace and the will is sufficient for a genuinely available contrary act, and what reason the examiners gave for the censure.

cases.next_source: Read Quesnel’s fuller passages on sufficient grace beside Báñez’s distinctions and the Roman votes on proposition 13.

audio.taught: Trent teaches that grace comes first and the will can assent or dissent. Báñez and Molina offer different accounts of what makes aid efficacious.
audio.authority: Paul the Fifth stopped the proceedings without promulgating a judgment choosing a school. Innocent the Tenth condemned the blanket claim that interior grace is never resisted.
audio.permanence: The Church’s teaching on grace and cooperation binds. The explanations of how divine action and free consent fit together remain disputed.

evidence_reviews.question: What claim do the two schools actually disagree about?
evidence_reviews.finding: Both attribute the supernatural aid to God. Molina says free cooperation is a condition for the aid’s efficacy relative to the effect. Báñez says the act of consent is the will’s own act and the grace that brings it about has its infallible efficacy from God.
evidence_reviews.test: Compare efficacy as divine causal power with efficacy in relation to the effect. Trace the different senses of power and actual dissent.

evidence_reviews.question: What does the Roman record rule out?
evidence_reviews.finding: Paul V forbade partisan censures. Innocent X explicitly disallows the purported acts and supposed constitution condemning Molina. Cum occasione separately censures the universal denial of resistance.
evidence_reviews.test: Distinguish the content of the promulgated acts from claims in circulated materials and from the theological positions themselves.

evidence_reviews.question: Does Quesnel’s distinction meet Trent’s test?
evidence_reviews.finding: He says resistance can hinder a further effect and describes the immediate effect intended by God as infallible. He invokes Thomist authorities and explicitly rejects the second proposition of Jansenius.
evidence_reviews.test: Ask what the aided person can actually refuse in the cases described. Similar language about God’s absolute will cannot decide that without comparing the scope of the two accounts and the Roman record.

log.change: Read selected Latin passages in Molina and Báñez, the Roman acts on the controversy, and Quesnel’s treatment of immediate and further effects.

cases.title: Quanta cura and the Syllabus beside Dignitatis Humanae
cases.question: Is the liberty Pius IX condemned the same proposition as the civil immunity from coercion that Dignitatis Humanae declares a right?
cases.summary: Gregory XVI called it "insanity" that liberty of conscience must be claimed for everyone, and Pius IX condemned the opinion that liberty of conscience and worship is each man's proper right, to be proclaimed in law in every well-ordered society. Vatican II declared that the human person has a right to religious freedom, an immunity from coercion within due limits, to be recognised in constitutional law. Benedict XVI used this as his example of reform in continuity: the condemnations rejected a liberty grounded in indifference to truth, the Council affirmed an immunity grounded in the dignity of the person, and the Council says it leaves the traditional doctrine on duties toward the true religion untouched. The case is substantial but contested; the words "proper right of every man ... proclaimed by law" come close to what the Council says.

texts.label: Pius IX, Quanta cura and the Syllabus (8 December 1864)
Benedict XVI, Address to the Roman Curia (22 December 2005)

propositions.quote: liberty of conscience and of worship is the proper right of every man, and should be proclaimed and asserted by law in every correctly established society
propositions.says: Condemned: that liberty of conscience and worship is every man's proper right, to be proclaimed in law, with a right to all manner of liberty unrestrained by any authority.
Syllabus 79, condemned: that civil liberty of every cult and full power to manifest any opinion does not lead more easily to corruption and indifferentism.

propositions.quote: liberty of conscience must be claimed and defended for anyone
propositions.says: Gregory XVI: from indifferentism flows the "insanity" that liberty of conscience must be claimed for anyone.

propositions.quote: the human person has a right to religious freedom
propositions.says: The person has a right to religious freedom: immunity from coercion by any human power, within due limits, founded in dignity, to be a civil right.
The Council leaves untouched the traditional doctrine on the moral duty of men and societies toward the true religion.
propositions.note: The sentence is in DH 1; check that the site's excerpt includes it.

matrix.why: Same predicate class ("right", "proclaimed by law"). Different grounds and objects: the condemned opinion grounds the right in a liberty unrestrained by any authority and joined to indifferentism; the Council grounds an immunity from coercion in the dignity of the person, within due limits of public order, and keeps the duty toward truth. Concord holds if the grounds and limits are part of the propositions; conflict if "right ... proclaimed by law" is the whole of each.
Syllabus 79 is a factual-prudential judgment (unlimited liberty leads more easily to corruption); the Council's immunity is limited by public order. Different predicates.

cases.qualifications: Quanta cura: the right "to all manner of liberty ... not to be restrained by either ecclesiastical or civil authority". Dignitatis Humanae: "within due limits"; "leaves untouched traditional Catholic doctrine".
cases.reception: John Courtney Murray and the majority at the Council read development; Archbishop Lefebvre and later traditionalist critics read rupture; Thomas Pink reads the earlier texts as about the Church's jurisdiction over the baptised, which the Council does not address; Basile Valuet catalogues the readings. Benedict XVI (2005) presents it as reform in continuity.
cases.contingency: Partly: the confessional State and the toleration Leo XIII allowed (1874) were contingent arrangements. The test does not apply to the claim of a natural right, which is doctrinal.
cases.development: What survives: the duty to seek and embrace the truth; the rejection of indifferentism; the freedom of the act of faith from coercion (Trent and earlier). What is new: the explicit civil right.
cases.hypothesis: The nineteenth-century acts condemned a right grounded in indifference to truth and unrestrained by any authority; the Council declared an immunity grounded in dignity, limited by public order and joined to the duty toward truth. These are different propositions. (T)
cases.objection: "Liberty of conscience and of worship is the proper right of every man, and should be proclaimed and asserted by law" is almost word for word what Dignitatis Humanae 2 declares. The distinction of grounds is supplied by the interpreter, not by Pius IX, who also condemned the claim (Syllabus 77–78) that other cults should be admitted in Catholic countries.
cases.rebuttal: The condemned sentence continues: a right "to all manner of liberty ... not to be restrained by either ecclesiastical or civil authority", which the Council does not assert. Syllabus 77–78 concern the confessional State in particular circumstances, a contingent arrangement (P5). The objection keeps its force against any claim that nothing changed; the site claims development, not identity.

gaps.what: The full sentence of DH 1 on the traditional doctrine
gaps.source: Dignitatis Humanae 1 (vatican.va)
gaps.settles: That b1-dh1 is quoted from the site's excerpt.

cases.next_source: The Latin of Quanta cura 3, to compare "ius proprium" with Dignitatis Humanae 2.
cases.benedict: Benedict XVI's own example: he names religious liberty as a case where contingent decisions changed while the principle continued. This case follows his judgment and is not an inference.

audio.taught: Pius IX condemned the idea that freedom of conscience and worship is everyone's right, to be written into law, with no authority able to limit it. The Second Vatican Council taught that everyone has a right not to be coerced in religion, within the limits of public order, and that this should be a civil right.
audio.authority: Papal encyclicals and the Syllabus on one side; a declaration of an ecumenical council on the other. Neither is a solemn definition.
audio.permanence: Permanent: the duty to seek the truth, and the freedom of the act of faith. Contingent: the confessional State. Disputed: whether the two texts speak of the same right.

log.change: Draft created from the texts the site holds; primary sources not yet verified against critical editions.

cases.title: Lateran IV, canon 3, beside Dignitatis Humanae
cases.question: Does a once-legitimate penal law against heretics conflict with a later right to religious freedom grounded in human dignity?
cases.summary: Lateran IV's canon 3 required secular powers to expel heretics from their lands, under ecclesiastical penalties. Dignitatis Humanae teaches that no one may be coerced in religion by any human power, as a right founded in dignity. If the canon was a juridical determination that bound in its time, and the Council's right is a natural right, then the canon commanded something the Council says is contrary to a natural right. That is a tension at the moral level, not only a change of law. Two readings try to remove it, neither yet established. The site does not hold the penal clauses of canon 3, so the case is at an early stage.

texts.label: Lateran IV, constitution 3 (1215): the necessity of a canonical mission
texts.note: The site's excerpt gives only the clause on unauthorised preaching, not the penal clauses on heretics.

propositions.says: Secular authorities are to be admonished and if necessary compelled by censure to expel heretics; a ruler who neglects it may be excommunicated and his vassals released.

propositions.quote: That heretics be burned is against the will of the Spirit
propositions.says: Luther's proposition 33 is among those condemned respectively.
No one may be forced to act against his beliefs by any human power, within due limits; the right is founded in the dignity of the person.

matrix.why: A law against a declared right: if the law's content is coercion of religious acts that the right forbids, the law commanded what is unjust. Two readings: (1) the law concerned the baptised under the Church's jurisdiction, which the Council's civil right does not address (Pink); (2) the law was an erroneous application of principle in its time, reformable because not definitive. The first is unproved from the text; the second concedes a moral error in a conciliar law.
Proposition 33 is condemned in globo; it may deserve only a light note, and its condemned sense may be the denial that the Church may punish at all.

cases.qualifications: Dignitatis Humanae: "within due limits"; it speaks of "any human power".
cases.reception: On the Day of Pardon (12 March 2000) John Paul II asked forgiveness for the use of violence in the service of truth. Pink argues for a jurisdictional reading; Murray for development; others for a reversal of a moral judgment.
cases.contingency: The law is plainly contingent and abrogated. The test does not reach the question whether it was ever just, which is a moral claim (stage 6 forbids using contingency as an escape here).

cases.title: Florence, the Holy Office and salvation outside the Church
cases.question: What kind of union with the Church is necessary for salvation, and how does the 1949 letter interpret that necessity?
cases.summary: Florence says that those outside the Catholic Church cannot share in eternal life unless they are joined to her before death. The Holy Office letter Suprema haec sacra, approved by Pius XII in 1949, distinguishes actual incorporation as a member from union by desire. In invincible ignorance that desire can be implicit. The letter requires perfect charity and supernatural faith. Lumen Gentium describes different relationships to the Church and cites the letter in its treatment of those who have yet to receive the Gospel.

texts.label: Boniface VIII, Unam Sanctam (1302)
texts.edition: Medieval Sourcebook, English text, with the Denzinger Latin.
texts.checked: The closing declaration makes subjection to the Roman Pontiff necessary for salvation. The bull also treats the Church as one body.

texts.label: Florence, Cantate Domino (4 February 1442)
texts.edition: Vatican Latin edition, union with the Copts.
texts.checked: The bull names several groups outside the Church, requires that they be joined to her before death and locates the saving fruit of the sacraments within the unity of her body.

texts.label: Pius IX, Quanto conficiamur (1863)
texts.edition: Vatican Italian edition, 10 August 1863.
texts.checked: Pius IX considers involuntary ignorance, life in accord with the moral law, readiness to obey God, and the operation of divine light and grace.

texts.label: Pius XII, Mystici Corporis §§22, 103 (1943)
texts.edition: Vatican English edition, 29 June 1943.
texts.checked: Pius XII distinguishes actual membership from the relation of some people to the Mystical Body through unrecognized yearning and desire.

texts.label: Holy Office, Suprema haec sacra (8 August 1949)
texts.edition: Protocol 122/49. English version published by Archbishop Richard Cushing under instructions from the Holy Office, Boston, 1952.
texts.checked: The letter calls the Church both a commanded end of incorporation and a necessary means of salvation. It allows implicit desire under specified conditions. It records Pius XII’s approval on 28 July 1949.

texts.label: Vatican II, Lumen Gentium §§14–16 (1964)
texts.edition: Vatican English edition, 21 November 1964, especially the note citing the Holy Office letter.
texts.checked: The council distinguishes Catholic incorporation, connection through baptism and gifts shared with other Christians, and the ways those without the Gospel are related to the people of God.

texts.label: Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, Dominus Iesus §§20–22 (2000)
texts.edition: Vatican English edition, 6 August 2000.
texts.checked: The declaration affirms that grace can reach those who are not formal and visible members through a relationship to the Church. It describes the way grace reaches individual persons as known to God.

propositions.says: Those outside the Catholic Church cannot share in eternal life unless they have been joined to her before death.
propositions.note: The Latin is nisi ante finem vite eidem fuerint aggregati. The bull speaks in the setting of an act of ecclesial reunion.

propositions.says: Boniface VIII declares subjection to the Roman Pontiff necessary for salvation.
Under divine light and grace, people who are invincibly ignorant and are disposed to obey God can attain eternal life.
Some outside the visible Catholic body are related to the Mystical Body through a yearning and desire of which they are unaware.
A person who knows that Christ founded the Church and nevertheless refuses submission cannot be saved.
propositions.ext: Holy Office, Suprema haec sacra, doctrinal explanation

propositions.says: Salvation requires at least union with the Church by desire. In invincible ignorance that desire can be implicit. It must be formed by perfect charity, and implicit desire requires supernatural faith.
propositions.ext: Holy Office, Suprema haec sacra, doctrinal explanation

propositions.says: The Church is necessary. Anyone who knows it was made necessary by Christ and refuses to enter or remain cannot be saved. Full incorporation without perseverance in charity also fails to save.
The Church recognizes several bonds with baptized Christians who are outside full communion.
Those who through no fault of their own do not know the Gospel or the Church, sincerely seek God and try under grace to do his will as known through conscience can attain salvation.
Saving grace for those outside formal visible membership has a relationship to the Church and comes from Christ in the Spirit.

matrix.why: Florence requires union before death. The Holy Office explains that actual membership and union by desire are distinct, and that in specified circumstances the latter can suffice. That is the later magisterial explanation of the dogma. The exact range of the term in Florence’s drafting is a historical question.

The Holy Office names the duty of submission and identifies knowing refusal as incompatible with salvation. It gives its account of implicit desire within the same explanation. The letter does not give a separate exegesis of every clause of Unam Sanctam.

The council describes the conditions under which people unaware of the Gospel may attain salvation and cites the Holy Office letter. The letter describes the union, faith and charity at issue. Neither passage specifies how grace produces these dispositions in each person.
Both texts distinguish a knowing refusal from the case of a person without knowledge of the Church. Both affirm the obligation to enter.

cases.qualifications: The letter distinguishes the divine command to enter the Church from the Church’s role as a means of salvation. A person’s desire may be implicit, but ignorance alone is insufficient. The letter requires proper dispositions and notes the loss of helps available within the Church.
cases.reception: At the Holy Office’s direction, Archbishop Cushing published the letter in 1952. Lumen Gentium cites the letter in §16. Dominus Iesus §§20–22 further explains the Church’s relation to saving grace and the duty of evangelization.
cases.contingency: The 1949 letter also addresses the conduct of the parties and applies the canon law then in force. Those disciplinary instructions have a different object from the explanation of the dogma.
cases.development: Florence’s necessity of union remains in view. Pius XII and the Holy Office articulate a relation to the Church through desire distinct from visible membership. Vatican II situates that teaching among the different ways people are related to the people of God.
cases.hypothesis: Florence’s requirement of union and the later account of non-visible union can be read together. The Holy Office’s account supplies the positive claim, including the role of faith, charity, and grace. (T)
cases.objection: Florence names people outside Catholic unity and requires aggregation before death. Does implicit desire satisfy the kind of union Florence actually requires, especially where the person does not know the Church?
cases.rebuttal: Suprema haec sacra expressly reads the dogma as requiring union and permits that union by desire in the specified circumstances. The council’s citation of the letter gives direct evidence of how later teaching received this explanation. The exact understanding of the Florence drafters and the manner in which supernatural faith is present in individual cases remain distinct questions.

gaps.what: The force and historical reception of aggregati in Florence
gaps.source: The drafting and sources of Cantate Domino, especially the use of Fulgentius, and early commentaries on the decree.
gaps.settles: How the decree’s reunion setting and source language bear on the precise form of union it requires.

gaps.what: The scope of supernatural faith in the case of implicit desire
gaps.source: The history of the Holy Office letter and studies of the drafting of Lumen Gentium §16 and Dominus Iesus §21.
gaps.settles: Which accounts of supernatural faith and implicit desire fit the conditions explicitly named in the acts.

cases.next_source: Trace the text of Lumen Gentium §16 and its citation of Suprema haec sacra through the conciliar drafts and relatio.

audio.authority: The Holy Office letter was approved by Pius the Twelfth. The Second Vatican Council cites it and describes different relationships to the people of God.
audio.permanence: The Church is necessary for salvation. The letter names supernatural faith and charity, and the application to particular people belongs to God.

cases.title: Cantate Domino, Nostra Aetate 4, and the covenant with Israel
cases.question: How do Florence's teaching on the ceremonies of the Law, Nostra Aetate 4 and later statements about the Jewish people and the covenant fit together?
cases.summary: Florence taught that the ceremonies of the Mosaic law ceased with Christ, and that after the promulgation of the Gospel they cannot be observed as necessary for salvation without mortal sin. Nostra Aetate 4 recalls the Church's bond with Abraham's stock, rejects the charge of deicide against the Jews as a people and deplores antisemitism; Lumen Gentium 16 and Evangelii Gaudium 247 speak of a covenant never revoked. Distinctions remove part of the tension: Florence speaks of observing the Law as necessary for salvation; the later texts speak of God's fidelity and of history, not of a separate way of salvation without Christ. Whether "never revoked" can be squared with Florence's "ceased" is not settled by these texts.

texts.label: Vatican II, Nostra Aetate 4 and Lumen Gentium 16
Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews, "The Gifts and the Calling of God are Irrevocable" (2015)

propositions.quote: placed hope in these matters of the law and submitted himself to them as necessary for salvation
propositions.says: The ceremonies of the Mosaic law ceased with Christ; whoever after the passion put hope in them as necessary for salvation sinned mortally; after the promulgation of the Gospel they cannot be observed without loss of eternal salvation.
The Church received the Old Testament through the people with whom God concluded the Ancient Covenant; the Jews are not to be presented as rejected or accursed.

propositions.quote: their covenant with God has never been revoked
propositions.says: The Jewish people's covenant with God has never been revoked.

matrix.why: Florence: the ceremonial law ceased as a way of worship and cannot be kept as necessary for salvation. Evangelii Gaudium: the covenant is not revoked. If "covenant" means God's election and promises (Rom 11:29), no conflict; if it means the Mosaic order of worship as salvific, conflict. Evangelii Gaudium cites Romans 11:29, which supports the first.
Nostra Aetate does not speak of observance of the Law as a means of salvation.

cases.qualifications: Florence: "as necessary for salvation"; "after the promulgation of the Gospel". Evangelii Gaudium: grounded in Romans 11:29.
cases.reception: The 2015 document of the Commission says the Church has no institutional mission to the Jews while holding that salvation is through Christ; critics on both sides read it as either too much or too little. Benedict XVI's 2018 article in Communio discussed "never revoked" and the "theory of substitution".
cases.contingency: Not applicable to the doctrine; the repudiation of antisemitism and of the deicide charge corrects historical attitudes and teaching (H).
cases.development: What survives: salvation through Christ alone; the ceremonial law fulfilled in him. What is clearer: God's fidelity to his election of Israel.
cases.hypothesis: Florence concerns the Mosaic ceremonies as a means of salvation; the later texts concern God's irrevocable election. No text teaches a separate salvific way without Christ. (T)
cases.objection: "Never revoked" in its natural sense denies the supersession Florence states ("ceased"), and the 2015 document's refusal of an institutional mission suggests in practice a separate way.
cases.rebuttal: The covenant language of Evangelii Gaudium rests on Romans 11:29, which Paul wrote while holding that the ceremonies do not justify. The concern about a separate way is about a commission document and practice, not about the conciliar or papal texts; it remains a live dispute.

gaps.what: The 2015 document, nos. 35–40
gaps.source: vatican.va, Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews
gaps.settles: Whether it asserts or denies a separate way.

cases.next_source: The 2015 Commission document.

audio.authority: A decree of an ecumenical council; a conciliar declaration; a papal exhortation.
audio.permanence: Permanent: salvation is through Christ; God keeps his promises. Unsettled: exactly what "covenant" means in each text.

cases.title: Mortalium animos and the 1927 decree beside Unitatis Redintegratio
cases.question: Does ecumenism imply the doctrinal indifferentism Pius XI condemned, or do different practices fall under one principle?
cases.summary: In 1927 the Holy Office forbade Catholics to take part in meetings that aimed to unite all who call themselves Christians on a single agreement, and Pius XI's Mortalium animos (1928) explained why: such meetings presumed that the Church of Christ does not yet exist and that unity is to be built out of the denominations, which is indifferentism. Vatican II's Unitatis Redintegratio encouraged Catholic participation in the ecumenical movement while warning against false irenicism and teaching a hierarchy of truths. The principle is the same, unity in the one Church and in the whole truth; the practice changed, and the Council explains why: the movement itself had changed, and Catholics were to take part without accepting its earlier premise.

texts.label: John Paul II, Ut Unum Sint (1995)

propositions.says: Catholics may not attend or take part in meetings of non-Catholics aiming to unite all who claim the name of Christian under a single agreement.
Such efforts presume that all religions or denominations are more or less good and that the Church of Christ is yet to be made; unity is return to the one true Church.

propositions.quote: in Catholic doctrine there exists a "hierarchy" of truths
propositions.says: Catholic theologians in dialogue stand fast by the Church's teaching; there is a hierarchy of truths; false irenicism is foreign to ecumenism.

matrix.why: A prohibition of participation in a particular kind of meeting, with a stated premise, against a permission to take part on Catholic principles. Different acts under the same principle.
Pius XI condemns indifferentism and the claim that the Church does not yet exist; the Council teaches that the Church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church and rejects false irenicism.

cases.qualifications: The 1927 decree concerns meetings "which aim to associate together under a single agreement all who in any way lay claim to the name of Christian".
cases.reception: Traditionalist critics read a reversal of practice as a reversal of doctrine; the common reading is development of discipline under the same doctrine (Congar, Ratzinger).
cases.contingency: Passes: the prohibition was a prudential and juridical determination tied to the premises of the movements of the 1920s.
cases.development: What survives: the one Church; unity as communion in the whole faith; rejection of indifferentism.
cases.hypothesis: One principle (unity in the truth of the one Church), two determinations under different conditions. (T)
cases.objection: The ecumenical movement Catholics joined after 1964 is the same World Council lineage Pius XI refused, and its premise did not change; so the practice now presumes what Mortalium animos condemned.
cases.rebuttal: Unitatis Redintegratio states Catholic participation on Catholic premises (UR 3, 4, 11), and Dominus Iesus (2000) restated the doctrine that Pius XI defended. Whether every ecumenical practice keeps to that is a question of prudence, not of contradiction between the texts.

gaps.source: AAS 20 (1928) 5–16; vatican.va
gaps.settles: Its exact premises.

audio.authority: A decree of the Holy Office and an encyclical; a conciliar decree.
audio.permanence: Permanent: unity in the one Church and the whole truth. Changed: the practical rule about taking part.

cases.title: Pastor aeternus and Lumen Gentium 22: collegiality and the primacy
cases.question: Is the episcopal college as a subject of supreme power consistent with the full Petrine jurisdiction Vatican I defined?
cases.summary: Vatican I defined that the pope has full and supreme jurisdiction over the whole Church, ordinary and immediate. Lumen Gentium 22 teaches that the order of bishops, together with its head and never without him, is also the subject of supreme and full power, which it cannot exercise without the pope's consent. The Preliminary Note of Explanation, added by Paul VI's order, says that the pope can always exercise his power freely and that the college never acts without its head. The texts were written to fit, and the Note is the authoritative key. The theological question of whether there are one or two subjects of supreme power remains open, but neither answer denies Vatican I.

texts.label: Vatican II, Lumen Gentium 22 and the Preliminary Note of Explanation

propositions.says: The Roman Pontiff has full and supreme, ordinary and immediate power of jurisdiction over the universal Church.
This power does not impede but asserts and strengthens the ordinary and immediate power of the bishops.
The order of bishops, with its head and never without him, is also the subject of supreme and full power over the universal Church, which it can exercise only with his consent.
"College" is not a group of equals; the pope can always exercise his power at will; the college does not act without its head.

matrix.why: Vatican I: the pope has full and supreme power. Lumen Gentium: the college with the pope has supreme power, exercised only with his consent. A second subject that includes the first and never acts without him does not limit him.

cases.qualifications: "Together with its head ... and never without this head"; "with the consent of the Roman Pontiff".
cases.reception: Rahner held one subject (the college with its head), the pope acting as its head; others hold two inadequately distinct subjects. Both are within the Note.
cases.contingency: Not applicable.
cases.development: Homogeneous: Vatican I's planned constitution on the Church was never finished; Lumen Gentium completes it.
cases.hypothesis: The two councils teach compatible propositions, and the Note fixes their relation. (D/T)
cases.objection: A college with supreme power, even with its head, is a second sovereign; Vatican I's "full" leaves no room for one.
cases.rebuttal: Vatican I itself says papal power "asserts, confirms and vindicates" episcopal power (n. 1828). A college that cannot act without the pope's consent takes nothing from fullness. The theoretical question of one or two subjects does not reach the definition.

gaps.what: The Latin of the Preliminary Note, n. 3–4
gaps.settles: The exact wording on the pope acting "ad placitum".

cases.next_source: The Note in AAS 57.

audio.authority: A conciliar definition, and a dogmatic constitution with an explanatory note added by papal order.
audio.permanence: Permanent: both. What theologians still discuss is whether these are one subject of authority or two.

cases.title: Quas primas and Immortale Dei beside Dignitatis Humanae: the State and religion
cases.question: How do the duties of States toward the true religion, as Leo XIII and Pius XI taught them, relate to permissible constitutional forms and to civil religious liberty?
cases.summary: Leo XIII taught that the State, like individuals, owes worship to God and must not treat all religions alike, while allowing rulers to tolerate other worships for a great good or to avoid evil; Pius XI's Quas primas taught that Christ's kingship extends to civil society. Dignitatis Humanae teaches civil immunity from coercion and says it leaves untouched the traditional doctrine on the moral duty of societies toward the true religion. This case shares propositions with B1 and C5 and is linked to them rather than repeating them. Its own question is constitutional form: the earlier texts do not bind a State to a particular legal establishment, and the Council allows a special civil recognition of one religion.

texts.label: Leo XIII, Immortale Dei (1885) and Libertas (1888)

propositions.says: The Church does not condemn rulers who, for a great good or to prevent an evil, tolerate various forms of worship.
Christ as man has power over all civil affairs; whoever denies it errs gravely.
The Council leaves untouched the traditional doctrine on the moral duty of men and societies toward the true religion and the one Church of Christ.

matrix.why: A moral duty of societies toward the true religion, affirmed by both; no specific legal establishment is required by either.
Leo XIII: toleration as a permitted concession. The Council: immunity as a right. Treated in C5.

cases.qualifications: Immortale Dei: toleration "to obtain some great blessing or to prevent an evil". Dignitatis Humanae 6: special civil recognition of one community is permitted, provided religious freedom is respected.
cases.reception: Murray read the earlier texts as tied to the nineteenth-century confessional State; integralist writers read them as permanent doctrine of the confessional State. The post-conciliar concordats (Italy 1984, Spain 1979) dropped confessional clauses.
cases.contingency: Passes for the form of establishment, which is a contingent arrangement; not for the moral duty, which both affirm.
cases.development: What survives: the social kingship of Christ and the duty of societies toward the true religion. Changed: the legal forms the Church seeks.
cases.hypothesis: The duty is doctrinal; its legal expression is a determination under circumstances. (T)
cases.objection: If the State owes public worship to the true religion, it cannot also be bound to give every religion equal immunity; Dignitatis Humanae's "untouched" is a formula that conceals a change.
cases.rebuttal: Dignitatis Humanae requires immunity from coercion, not equal honour; it allows special recognition. The objection identifies a real pressure between the texts in their emphasis, which this site records in B1 and C5.

gaps.settles: The Council's own allowance for establishment.

audio.permanence: Permanent: the duty of societies toward the truth. Contingent: the legal arrangement between Church and State.

cases.title: The death penalty: Innocent III, Evangelium Vitae and Catechism 2267 (2018)
cases.question: Does "inadmissible" in the revised Catechism 2267 name an intrinsic moral object, or a judgment about changed conditions and penal options?
cases.summary: In 1210 Innocent III required the Waldensians to accept that secular power may impose the death penalty without mortal sin, provided it acts in judgment, not hatred. John Paul II taught in 1995 that it should not go to that extreme except in cases of absolute necessity, which today are very rare if not non-existent. In 2018 the Catechism was revised to say that the death penalty "is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person". The revised text gives two kinds of reason: changes of fact (better systems of detention, a new understanding of penal sanctions) and the dignity of the person. If the first governs, the change is a prudential application and no definitive teaching is touched. If the second means the penalty is wrong in itself, it contradicts 1210. The text supports both readings, and so does the commentary on it; the site marks the case unresolved.

texts.label: Innocent III, profession of faith for the Waldensians (1208, clause added 1210)
Catechism of the Catholic Church 2267, revised (1 August 2018)
Doctrine of the Faith, letter to the bishops on the revision (2 August 2018)

propositions.quote: without mortal sin it is possible to exercise a judgment of blood
propositions.says: Secular power can exercise a judgment of blood without mortal sin, if it punishes in judgment and not in hatred, advisedly and not rashly.
propositions.note: A clause in a profession imposed on returning Waldensians; its grade is disputed (definitive teaching on a moral matter, or an authentic statement in a particular profession).

propositions.quote: except in cases of absolute necessity
propositions.says: Punishment ought not go to the extreme of execution except in cases of absolute necessity, which today are very rare if not practically non-existent.

propositions.quote: more effective systems of detention have been developed
propositions.says: Reasons of fact: awareness of dignity after crime, a new understanding of penal sanctions, more effective systems of detention.

propositions.quote: the death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person
propositions.says: The death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person.

matrix.why: Innocent III: the penalty can be imposed without sin under conditions. The revised 2267 on its factual reasons: today the conditions are not met. Different circumstances.

If "attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person" means that any execution is evil in its object, it denies what Innocent III required the Waldensians to profess. If "inadmissible" means "not to be admitted under present conditions", there is no conflict. The word inadmissibilis is not a term of the moral tradition and does not decide.

cases.qualifications: 1210: "not in hatred but in judgment, not incautiously but advisedly". 1995: "absolute necessity". 2018: "Today, however ... Consequently".
cases.reception: Feser and Bessette argue that the traditional teaching is irreformable and read 2267 as prudential; others (e.g., the 2018 letter's own framing as "authentic development") read it as a deeper grasp of dignity; some moralists hold it now teaches intrinsic evil. Fratelli Tutti 263–270 restates the position without settling the category.
cases.contingency: Applies to the factual reasons and passes for them. It may not be used to dissolve the dignity clause if that clause states an intrinsic moral claim (stage 6 rule).
cases.development: If the factual reading holds, what survives is the State's authority to punish in proportion and the right of legitimate defence. If the intrinsic reading holds, an earlier moral claim would be denied; the site does not count that as development.
cases.hypothesis: The revision is a moral application grounded in changed conditions and a deeper grasp of dignity, not a declaration that the penalty is intrinsically evil. (T)
cases.objection: The decisive clause gives dignity as the reason, and dignity does not change with prison systems. A penalty that attacks the inviolability of the person is wrong whenever it is inflicted, so the revision teaches that what the Church allowed for eight centuries was always wrong.
cases.rebuttal: The same paragraph introduces its conclusion with "Consequently", after factual reasons, and the Church has not called the penalty intrinsically evil in the terms Veritatis Splendor 80 uses. But the objection has textual weight that this site cannot remove, and the Holy See has not resolved it.

gaps.source: press.vatican.va, 2 August 2018
gaps.settles: Whether the Congregation frames the change as application or as a new moral norm.

gaps.what: The grade of the 1210 clause
gaps.source: The Waldensian profession in its setting; DH 795
gaps.settles: Whether it is definitive.

cases.title: Usury: Vix pervenit and modern interest
cases.question: Is the condemnation of usury as an injustice in the loan itself kept, or reversed, by the modern acceptance of interest?
cases.summary: Benedict XIV defined usury as taking profit from a loan by reason of the loan itself, which of its nature requires only the return of what was lent; such profit is unjust. He allowed that extrinsic titles can justify more, and that money can be invested in contracts other than lending. Lateran V had approved moderate charges by the Mountains of Piety. The principle has not been withdrawn. What changed is economic reality: when money is ordinarily productive, risk and lost opportunity become ordinary titles. The application changed under the same principle.

texts.label: Lateran V, on the Mountains of Piety (1515)

propositions.quote: from the loan itself, which of its very nature demands that only as much be returned as was received
propositions.says: Usury: profit from the loan itself, beyond the principal, by reason of the loan; all such profit is unlawful.

propositions.quote: certain other titles
propositions.says: Extrinsic titles can justly ground a demand beyond the principal; money can rightly be invested in other contracts for honest profit.
Lateran V defines that the Mountains of Piety, charging a moderate sum for expenses, are not usurious.
Lateran II condemns the rapacity of moneylenders and excludes them from ecclesiastical consolation.

matrix.why: The same encyclical: profit by reason of the loan as such is unjust; profit by reason of an extrinsic title is not. Modern interest is justified on the second ground.
A penal law against moneylenders, abrogated; the moral principle it served is kept in 1745.

cases.qualifications: "From the loan itself"; "by reason of the lending"; "titles ... not at all innate or intrinsic in general to the nature of a loan".
cases.reception: The Holy Office in the nineteenth century answered that those taking moderate legal interest were not to be disturbed (non esse inquietandos); the 1917 Code (canon 1543) allowed a legal rate where there is a just title. Some, e.g., John Noonan, read a real change of moral teaching; others read a change of fact.
cases.contingency: Passes: the economic conditions that make titles ordinary changed (H).
cases.development: What survives: a loan as such does not earn; exploitation of need is unjust.
cases.hypothesis: The principle of Vix pervenit is kept; its application changed with the nature of money and credit. (T)
cases.objection: For centuries the Church condemned charging for a loan of money in itself, not only exploitation, and modern finance charges for the loan as such; calling every interest payment an extrinsic title is a fiction that empties the principle.
cases.rebuttal: Vix pervenit itself names the titles and other contracts; what changed is how often they apply. The objection is strongest against consumer lending where no title exists beyond the loan, where the principle still bites.

gaps.settles: How Rome applied the principle to legal interest.

audio.authority: An encyclical letter, with earlier conciliar canons and Lateran V's decree on the Mountains of Piety.
audio.permanence: Permanent: a loan as such does not earn, and exploiting need is unjust. Contingent: how often other titles apply, which changed with the economy.

cases.title: Slavery: Dum diversas, Sublimis Deus, In supremo apostolatus
cases.question: How do papal grants of servitude, papal condemnations of enslavement and the later teaching that slavery is an infamy relate: authorisation, tolerated legal status, condemnation, principle?
cases.summary: Nicholas V's Dum diversas (1452) granted the King of Portugal power to reduce Saracens and pagans to perpetual servitude. Paul III's Sublimis Deus (1537) declared that the Indians and all peoples may not be deprived of liberty or property. Gregory XVI's In supremo apostolatus (1839) condemned the slave trade. Gaudium et Spes 27 lists slavery among infamies, and Veritatis Splendor 80 lists it among acts intrinsically evil. None of the three early bulls is on the site, so the case is at the first stage. The tension is plain: a grant of perpetual servitude implies a judgment that such servitude may be imposed; the later teaching calls it intrinsically evil. Distinctions between penal servitude, just-war captivity and chattel slavery may narrow the tension, but they must be shown from the bulls, not assumed.

texts.label: Nicholas V, Dum diversas (18 June 1452) and Romanus Pontifex (1455)
Gregory XVI, In supremo apostolatus (3 December 1839)

propositions.says: Grant to the King of Portugal to invade, subdue and reduce to perpetual servitude Saracens and pagans.
propositions.note: Text not on the site; wording to be verified.

propositions.says: The Indians and all other peoples, even outside the faith, are not to be deprived of their liberty or property, and are not to be enslaved.
Condemns the trade in slaves, Black or of any race, as unworthy of the Christian name.

propositions.quote: intrinsically evil
propositions.says: Acts by their object intrinsically evil, among which Gaudium et Spes 27 lists slavery.
propositions.note: The list itself is in GS 27 and in VS 80; check that the site's excerpts include it.

matrix.why: If Dum diversas authorises an act intrinsically evil, a papal act commanded or permitted evil; if the servitude it grants is penal servitude after a just war, a different object is at issue. Neither can be decided until the bull is read in full.
A grant of servitude over pagans against a declaration that peoples outside the faith may not be enslaved. Different addressees and circumstances; the principle in conflict is the same.

cases.qualifications: To be extracted from the bulls.
cases.reception: Panzer and Maxwell read the history in opposite directions (a consistent condemnation; a long toleration); Noonan counts slavery as a case of moral teaching that changed.
cases.contingency: Not to be applied to escape the intrinsic-evil claim (stage 6 rule). A juridical grant is abrogated; its moral premise is the question.
cases.development: Undetermined.
cases.hypothesis: None yet. The site will not propose a reconciliation before the bulls are read. (U)
cases.objection: A pope granted a king power to enslave pagans in perpetuity; the Church now teaches slavery is intrinsically evil. That is a reversal of moral judgment in papal acts.
cases.rebuttal: Not yet attempted.

gaps.settles: What was granted, over whom, on what ground.

gaps.settles: The scope of each condemnation.

audio.permanence: Permanent: the later teaching that slavery is intrinsically evil. Unresolved: how the earlier grant relates to it. This site has not yet read the earlier bulls in full.

cases.title: Inquisitorial law and the condemnation of torture
cases.question: Were the medieval rules allowing torture in inquisitorial procedure merely juridical, or did they assert a universal moral claim that later teaching denies?
cases.summary: Nicholas I told the Bulgarians in 866 that confessions extracted by torture are against divine and human law. Innocent IV's Ad extirpanda (1252) allowed civil authorities to use torture on heretics to extract confession, within limits. Gaudium et Spes 27 lists "torments inflicted on body or mind" among infamies, and Veritatis Splendor 80 counts physical and mental torture among acts intrinsically evil. The texts on torture are not on the site, so this case is at an early stage. As with slavery, a permission in a papal law appears to contradict a later claim of intrinsic evil; whether the permission asserted a moral proposition must be shown from its text.

texts.label: Nicholas I, Responsa ad consulta Bulgarorum 86 (866)
Vatican II, Gaudium et Spes 27; John Paul II, Veritatis Splendor 80

propositions.says: Confession extracted by torture is against divine and human law; a confession must be voluntary.
The podestà may compel heretics by torture, short of loss of limb or danger of death, to confess and accuse accomplices.
Physical and mental torture are among acts intrinsically evil (citing GS 27).

matrix.why: A papal law permitting torture against a teaching that torture is intrinsically evil. If the law asserts that torture so limited is morally permissible, conflict; if it only regulated a practice of civil courts, the conflict is between a moral claim and a law, not between two moral claims. Undecided until the text is read.
Nicholas I and John Paul II reject coerced confession on the same ground.

cases.qualifications: Ad extirpanda: "citra membri diminutionem et mortis periculum" (to be verified).
cases.reception: Historians of canon law (Kuttner, Peters) treat the permission as reception of Roman procedure; moralists differ on whether a moral claim was implied.
cases.contingency: Not to be used to dissolve an intrinsic-evil claim (stage 6 rule).
cases.development: Undetermined.
cases.hypothesis: None yet. (U)
cases.objection: A pope permitted torture by law; the Church now teaches torture is intrinsically evil.
cases.rebuttal: Not yet attempted. Note that the earlier condemnation by Nicholas I shows the principle was known and taught before the permission.

gaps.settles: What was permitted and on what ground.

cases.title: Toleration or right: Mirari vos, Quanta cura, Dignitatis Humanae
cases.question: Is civil religious liberty only a contingent concession, tolerated for the common good, or a positive right?
cases.summary: Leo XIII allowed rulers to tolerate other worships for a great good or to avoid an evil; the nineteenth-century texts treat such liberty as at most a concession. Dignitatis Humanae declares a right, founded in the dignity of the person, to immunity from coercion. A right is more than a concession; so the Council says something the earlier texts did not. The question is whether it denies anything they taught. They denied a right to all manner of liberty unrestrained by any authority, grounded in indifference; the Council declares a right to immunity, limited by public order, grounded in dignity and joined to the duty toward truth. This case shares its texts with B1 and B7 and is linked to them.

texts.label: Leo XIII, Immortale Dei (1885) and Libertas (1888)

propositions.says: The Church does not condemn rulers who tolerate other worships to obtain a great good or prevent an evil.
It is by no means lawful to demand, defend or grant unconditional freedom of thought, speech, writing or worship as if these were rights given by nature.
The right to religious freedom has its foundation in the dignity of the person, known by revelation and reason, and is to become a civil right.

matrix.why: Libertas: unconditional freedom of worship is not a natural right. Dignitatis Humanae: immunity from coercion within due limits is a right founded in nature (dignity). Concord if "unconditional" and "within due limits" mark different propositions; conflict if the Council's right is the same freedom Leo denied.
Toleration answers "may the State permit?"; the right answers "may the State coerce?". The second is a further question, not the contradictory of the first.

cases.qualifications: Libertas: "unconditional"; Dignitatis Humanae: "within due limits", "immunity from coercion".
cases.reception: As B1.
cases.contingency: Partly: toleration is a prudential category; the right is not.
cases.development: The Council adds a right the nineteenth-century texts did not assert; it denies a right they did not deny only if the propositions are the same.
cases.hypothesis: Development: toleration and right answer different questions; the right the Council declares is not the unconditional freedom Leo XIII denied. (T)
cases.objection: Leo XIII denied that freedom of worship is a natural right; the Council affirms that it is. "Unconditional" is doing too much work.
cases.rebuttal: Leo's sentence denies a right to "unconditional" freedom of "thought, speech, writing or worship" as if all were equally natural rights; the Council affirms a limited immunity. The objection is strongest if the Council's "due limits" are only public order and not truth, which the Council itself does not claim to settle beyond DH 1.

gaps.settles: The scope of "unconditional".

audio.authority: Encyclicals; a conciliar declaration.
audio.permanence: Permanent: the dignity of the person and the duty toward truth. The live question is whether the right the Council declares is the same thing Leo denied.

cases.title: Providentissimus Deus, Divino afflante Spiritu and Dei Verbum
cases.question: What is immutable about biblical inspiration and truth while methods of interpretation develop?
cases.summary: Leo XIII taught that inspiration excludes all error, not only in faith and morals, and Benedict XV rejected restricting it. Pius XII told interpreters to discern the literary forms the sacred writers used. Dei Verbum 11 teaches that the books teach "firmly, faithfully and without error that truth which God wanted put into sacred writings for the sake of salvation". Whether "for the sake of salvation" limits what is inerrant, or describes the purpose of all of it, is the open question. The Council's footnotes cite Augustine, Aquinas, Trent, Providentissimus and Divino afflante, which favours the second reading.

propositions.quote: not only excludes all error
propositions.says: Inspiration not only excludes all error but excludes it as necessarily as God cannot be the author of error.
Those err who think the historical parts depend not on the absolute truth of facts but on the opinion of the multitude.
The interpreter must discern the character, age, sources and forms of expression of the sacred writer.

propositions.quote: without error that truth which
propositions.says: The books teach firmly, faithfully and without error the truth God wished put into them for the sake of our salvation.

matrix.why: Leo XIII: no error at all. Dei Verbum: without error the truth for the sake of salvation. If "for the sake of salvation" restricts the domain, a narrower claim replaces a wider one; if it describes the purpose, both say the same. The Council's notes and the relatio support the second; the text alone does not decide.
Both teach that what the writer asserts depends on his literary form; inerrancy attaches to what is asserted.

cases.qualifications: Dei Verbum 11: "everything asserted by the inspired authors must be held to be asserted by the Holy Spirit".
cases.reception: Brown and others read a restriction; Grillmeier's commentary reads purpose; the 2014 Biblical Commission document The Inspiration and Truth of Sacred Scripture discusses both.
cases.contingency: Not applicable: doctrine of inspiration. Methods are contingent; the doctrine is not.
cases.development: What survives: God is author of all Scripture; what the writers assert, the Spirit asserts; Scripture is without error in what it asserts.
cases.hypothesis: Dei Verbum describes the purpose of Scripture's truth and applies the literary-form principle of Divino afflante; it does not restrict inerrancy to salvific matters. (T)
cases.objection: The final text dropped "salutaris" as an adjective of truth only after debate, and the phrase "for the sake of our salvation" was kept precisely to qualify what is inerrant; many exegetes and some bishops took it so.
cases.rebuttal: The change from "veritas salutaris" to "veritatem quam Deus nostrae salutis causa" was made, per the relatio, to avoid the restrictive reading. That is evidence for the purpose reading; the objection is a live school dispute, not a contradiction of Leo XIII.

gaps.source: Acta Synodalia IV/5
gaps.settles: Why the wording was changed.

audio.taught: Leo XIII taught that Scripture, inspired by God, contains no error at all. Pius XII told scholars to pay attention to literary forms. The Second Vatican Council taught that Scripture teaches without error the truth God wanted written for our salvation.
audio.authority: Encyclicals and a dogmatic constitution.
audio.permanence: Permanent: God is the author of Scripture and it asserts no error. Developing: methods of interpretation. Debated: whether "for our salvation" limits or explains.
