research_sources.citation: G. Bazin, Vie de Mgr Maret III (1891), pp. 218–219.
research_sources.note: Maret interpreted the final definition as compatible with episcopal concurrence and explained why he could accept it. The explanation is his interpretation of the definition.

research_sources.title: Palanque on the French reception of Vatican I
research_sources.citation: Jean-Rémy Palanque, Catholiques libéraux et gallicans en France face au Concile du Vatican, 1867–1870 (1962), pp. 185–186.
research_sources.note: The supplied extract describes how Abbé Bernard and other French Catholics understood the first three chapters when accepting the constitution.

research_sources.title: Eugene IV’s letter to the doge of Venice
research_sources.citation: Deutsche Reichstagsakten XI, pp. 67–68. Compare the second Dudum sacrum (B2) and the later letter to Basel (B20).
research_sources.note: Eugene disputed the proposed wording at that point in the negotiations. In December he used decree and declaration language to recognise the council’s continuation. The sequence sharpens the question of which legal effects the final bull conferred.

research_sources.title: Antonio Roselli claims authorship of Deus novit
research_sources.citation: Florence, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Plut. 16.13, letter beginning at fol. 128r. The passage is at fol. 129r. Valois transcribes it in La crise religieuse du XVe siècle I (1909), p. 289 n. 2.
research_sources.note: Roselli calls it epistola a me confecta quae incipit Deus novit, the letter he drafted which begins Deus novit. He reports that papal legates attributed the authorship to him alone during the dispute at Basel. The manuscript establishes his claim to authorship. Papal authorisation is a further historical question.

research_sources.title: Noël Valois on the authorship and circulation of Deus novit
research_sources.citation: La crise religieuse du XVe siècle I (1909), pp. 252–260 and p. 289 n. 2.
research_sources.note: Valois identifies Roselli as the drafter and cites testimony that the letter circulated in France through papal envoys. He finds some overlap with Eugene’s position and also differences. A witness to circulation can establish how a text was presented. Evidence of formal approval would have to come from an authentic papal act or reliable contemporary testimony about authorisation.

research_sources.title: Juan de Segovia on Basel’s examination of Deus novit
research_sources.citation: Historia gestorum generalis synodi Basiliensis VI.19, Monumenta conciliorum generalium II (1873), p. 499.
research_sources.note: Segovia reports that some theologians and jurists called the letter erroneous and others called it heretical, blasphemous, seditious or scandalous. Their conclusions were reported in the deputations. He says no express synodal definition was issued then, and explains why many thought a public revocation would suffice in the proceedings on faith.

research_sources.title: Stieber on Nicholas V’s confirmation
research_sources.citation: Joachim W. Stieber, Pope Eugenius IV, the Council of Basel and the Secular and Ecclesiastical Authorities in the Empire (1978), p. 303 n. 49.
research_sources.note: The supplied reference reports a further confirmation dated 2 August 1447, reciting specified instruments word for word. The original confirmation would help establish whether anything beyond those instruments was received (B16).

research_sources.title: Huguccio and the gloss on Si papa
research_sources.citation: Huguccio, Summa on Distinction 40, canon 6, in Brian Tierney, Foundations of the Conciliar Theory, pp. 248–250. Compare Johannes Teutonicus, Glossa ordinaria, Rome 1582, cols. 260–261.
research_sources.note: In the supplied excerpts, some canonists extend the question beyond doctrinal heresy to notorious scandal and refusal of correction after warning. Their reasoning supplies a historically available argument. The canonists differ over the conditions and procedure.

research_sources.title: Stump on correction and the Romanus pontifex draft
research_sources.role: Modern study of Constance’s reform proposals
research_sources.citation: Phillip H. Stump, The Reforms of the Council of Constance (1414–1418) (1994), pp. 132–135, 225–226, 232 and 267.
research_sources.note: The supplied excerpts connect schism, reform and the contemporary language of incorrigibility. The proposed procedure for warning and judging a pope was abandoned before enactment.

research_sources.title: Cesarini and Nicholas of Cusa on Basel
research_sources.citation: Gerald Christianson, Cardinal Cesarini and Cusa’s Concordantia, Church History 54 (1985), pp. 7–19.
research_sources.note: The supplied excerpts describe Cesarini’s use of faith, schism and reform and his objection to dissolving Basel. They also show that these arguments went beyond the problem of an uncertain papal title.

research_sources.title: Mattia Ugoni on appeals and papal correction
research_sources.citation: De conciliis: Synodia (Venice, 1568), fols. 111, 123–130.
research_sources.note: Ugoni reads Si papa broadly under conditions of notoriety, scandal and incorrigibility. He applies this reading to Constance and argues for exceptions to Exsecrabilis. The publication approval and his argument have different evidentiary force.

research_sources.title: Francisco de Vitoria on conciliar decrees and dispensation
research_sources.citation: De potestate papae et concilii, ed. P. Landry (Lyon, 1586), pp. 133–136, 144–145 and 151–153. See also the commentary on Aquinas’s Secunda Secundae edited by Cándido Pozo, Archivo teológico granadino 25 (1962), pp. 278–282.
research_sources.note: The supplied excerpts distinguish defining faith and divine law from governing through ecclesiastical statutes. Vitoria also distinguishes mistaking or abusing the exercise of jurisdiction from lacking jurisdiction, including when discussing papal dispensations.

research_sources.title: Sutri and the conflicting accounts of Gregory VI
research_sources.role: Historical precedent debated in later sources
research_sources.citation: Peter Damian, Letter 72, PL 145, col. 441. See Jacques van Wijnendaele, Silences et mensonges autour d’un concile (2005).
research_sources.note: Peter Damian reports a deposition. Other witnesses describe a resignation or contest the legitimacy of the action. The accounts leave the officeholder’s title, the effect of simony and the competence of Henry III and the synod open (S2, S7–S9).

research_sources.title: Leonardo Dati on jurisdiction and its exercise
research_sources.citation: Debate at Constance, in Heinrich Finke, Acta Concilii Constanciensis II (1923), pp. 719–720.
research_sources.note: Dati distinguishes the Church’s capacity for jurisdiction from its exercise. He argues for the latter in the absence of a legitimate pope and applies his reasoning to John XXIII. This is evidence of a contemporary rationale for Constance’s acts.

research_sources.title: Gregory XII’s authorisation and the charges against John XXIII
research_sources.citation: Constance sessions 10–11 and 14. Von der Hardt IV, cols. 200, 205, 230–235 and 370–378.
research_sources.note: The articles against John record allegations of prior warnings and incorrigibility. Gregory’s act authorises the assembly under his own title in session 14. Read the articles, the sentence and the later authorisation as separate acts.

evidence_reviews.question: How far do the obedience and penal clauses of Haec Sancta reach?
evidence_reviews.finding: The obedience clause names faith, the ending of the schism and general reform, and expressly includes papal dignity. The penal clause reaches any lawfully assembled general council on those matters and requires contumacy. The text makes no reference to uncertainty of title. Gerson applied the decree to the pope in matters of faith. Pierre de Versailles distinguished a duty to heed a decree from the power to enforce it (Cedula Beati Pauli apostoli vox, ed. Thomas Prügl, pp. 124–126).
evidence_reviews.test: Establish the tribunal’s competence independently of any refusal to recognise it. Test what evidence supports the proposed distinction between directive and coercive force when the pope’s title is certain. Seek a witness linking Martin V’s qualified approval specifically to the constitutional claims of Haec Sancta.

evidence_reviews.question: Can notorious scandal cause loss of an otherwise valid papal title?
evidence_reviews.finding: The broader proposal treats grave, notorious and incorrigible scandal as legally analogous to heresy. Some medieval canonists give grounds for that analogy. Dati’s argument about exercise of jurisdiction supplies a historically attested mechanism where the pope is absent, illegitimate or deposed.
evidence_reviews.test: Prove independently that the alleged misconduct either caused loss of office or gave a competent body authority to declare it. A legal analogy or refusal to obey a disputed tribunal alone leaves the premise open. Test scandal, doctrinal heresy and disputed title separately.

evidence_reviews.question: Who wrote Deus novit, and what authority did it have?
evidence_reviews.finding: Roselli says he drafted the letter. It circulated in Eugene’s name and calls Basel’s claimed continuation heretical. At Basel some reviewers called the letter itself heretical. Segovia records their deliberations and says the council made no express synodal definition at the time. Eugene denied that the letter issued from him or with his knowledge, revoked it as a precaution, and declared Basel lawfully continued. D1 assigns the letter no papal magisterial weight on the present evidence.
evidence_reviews.test: Assess the claim that Eugene shared Roselli’s views against his authenticated acts, one proposition at a time. Treating Deus novit as a papal act would require independent evidence of authorisation. A formal censure by Basel would require a corresponding act of the council.

evidence_reviews.question: What did papal reception give legal force at Basel?
evidence_reviews.finding: The second Dudum sacrum recognised continuity in forceful terms. The 1446 reservation and the narrower 1447 concession support excluding session 11’s general rule. The Venice letter and the final bull record different moments in the negotiations.
evidence_reviews.test: Read the final legal act alongside the reserved rights and the specified decrees. Check the original of Nicholas V’s reported August 1447 confirmation for any broader reception.

evidence_reviews.question: What does Vatican I permit the historical explanations to claim?
evidence_reviews.finding: Pastor aeternus excludes a higher court over the reigning pope. Zinelli’s report explains the pope’s authority alone and with the bishops. It anticipates that remedies would be available in hypothetical emergencies and leaves them unspecified. The proposed extension of Pierre de Versailles’s habitual mediation to a coercive remedy remains a theological inference.
evidence_reviews.test: Test a procedure for restoring the office and an appeal from the judgment of its lawful holder separately. An appeal that falls under chapter 3’s prohibition cannot be justified by the emergency itself or by appealing to habitual mediation.

cases.title: Honorius I, Constantinople III and Vatican I
cases.question: What did Honorius teach and direct in his letters, what did the council and Leo II judge, and do the letters meet Vatican I’s conditions?
cases.summary: Honorius confessed one will in Christ while arguing from the absence of sinful conflict in Christ’s humanity. He urged Sergius and other bishops to avoid the formulas of one or two operations. John IV later defended the reference to one will. Constantinople III rejected Honorius’s letter and said he had confirmed Sergius’s impious teachings. Leo II confirmed the council and anathematized Honorius. His letter to the Spanish bishops faults him for fostering error by negligence, while the letter to the emperor has a stronger Latin reading alongside the Greek wording. The letters have a doctrinal and governing purpose. The surviving text gives no universal definition of the kind Vatican I specifies.

texts.label: Honorius I, two replies to Sergius (c. 634)
texts.edition: Mansi XI, acts XII–XIII. First letter Scripta fraternitatis and surviving passages of the second letter. Patrologia Latina 80, epistles IV–V.
texts.checked: The first letter confesses one will and gives a reason drawn from Christ’s sinlessness. The second directs the parties away from either formula for operations and acknowledges the proper activity of both natures.

texts.label: John IV, Dominus qui dixit (641)
texts.edition: Denzinger Latin and English, from John IV’s imperial letter.
texts.checked: John defends Honorius by explaining the single will as the absence of contrary wills of flesh and mind within Christ’s assumed humanity.

texts.label: Constantinople III, session XIII, judgment (681)
texts.edition: Mansi XI, cols. 553–556, Greek and Latin.
texts.checked: The judgment rejects the correspondence and anathematizes Honorius on the ground that in following Sergius he confirmed impious teachings.

texts.label: Constantinople III, sessions XVI and XVIII (681)
texts.edition: Mansi XI, the acclamations in session XVI and the definition in session XVIII. Denzinger for the definition.
texts.checked: Session XVI acclaims anathema to Honorius the heretic. The definition establishes two natural wills and two natural operations in the one Christ.

texts.label: Leo II, confirmation to Emperor Constantine IV (682–683)
texts.edition: Mansi XI, cols. 731–732, and Patrologia Latina 96, epistle III, cols. 407–408.
texts.checked: Leo receives the council and includes Honorius in his anathema. The printed Latin says he attempted to overturn the immaculate faith. The alternate Greek wording speaks of permitting it to be stained.

texts.label: Leo II, letter to the Spanish bishops (682–683)
texts.edition: Mansi XI, cols. 1051–1052, and Patrologia Latina 96, epistle IV, col. 414.
texts.checked: Leo says Honorius failed to extinguish heresy at its inception and fostered it by negligence.

texts.label: Vatican I, Pastor aeternus, chapter 4 (1870)
texts.edition: Vatican Latin edition, 18 July 1870, chapter 4, final definition.
texts.checked: The defining act must concern faith or morals, be made in the exercise of the office of pastor and teacher of all Christians by supreme apostolic authority, and propose a doctrine to be held by the universal Church.

propositions.says: Honorius confesses one will in Christ and explains it by Christ’s assumption of human nature without sin or the conflict of the flesh.
propositions.note: His letter also treats scriptural statements about Christ’s will in relation to the assumed humanity. The scope of his use of one will is disputed.

propositions.says: Honorius directs the parties away from preaching one or two operations and confesses that Christ operates what is proper to each nature.
propositions.note: The surviving passages mention directions to Cyrus and Sophronius. The reply has official purposes beyond a private opinion.

propositions.says: John IV explains his predecessor as denying internal opposition between the will of the flesh and the will of the mind in Christ.
The council rejects the correspondence and anathematizes Honorius because it found that he followed Sergius and confirmed his impious doctrines.
Christ has two natural wills and two natural operations. His human will follows the divine will without opposition.
Leo II confirms the council and also anathematizes Honorius. His letter to the emperor attributes a grave injury to apostolic faith.
propositions.ext: Leo II, confirmation to Constantine IV
propositions.note: The printed Latin and Greek differ in how they express Honorius’s agency. The act of anathematizing him is explicit.

propositions.says: Leo II tells the Spanish bishops that Honorius fostered heresy through negligence instead of extinguishing it.
Papal infallibility applies when the pope, acting as pastor and teacher of all Christians by supreme apostolic authority, defines a doctrine of faith or morals to be held by the whole Church.

matrix.why: If one will means only one natural will altogether, it conflicts with the definition. John IV reads it as the absence of a contrary, disordered will in Christ’s humanity. Honorius’s argument about sin supports that reading, while his general wording and the council’s judgment require attention.

The earlier letter tells bishops to set aside disputed terminology. The later council defines which terminology expresses the faith. The later definition settles a question that Honorius had sought to quiet.

The council explicitly says the writings confirmed Sergius’s doctrine. That establishes the council’s judgment. How its conclusion bears on Honorius’s private intention requires evidence from his complete arguments.

The conciliar finding concerns the effect of what Honorius wrote. The Spanish letter describes how he fostered the error by failing to suppress it. Leo’s explicit confirmation to the emperor includes the anathema.

The letter addresses a matter of faith and is official correspondence. There is no evidence that it purports to use supreme apostolic authority as teacher of all Christians to define a doctrine required of the whole Church.
The posthumous sentence concerns Honorius and his letters, and Leo II confirms it. Vatican I’s definition concerns a specified type of papal act. It gives no procedure for judging a reigning pope.

cases.qualifications: The acts distinguish a Christological definition, a posthumous sentence and its confirmation, and the terms of a papal reply. The stronger wording of the Latin confirmation and Leo’s wording about negligence both belong in the account.
cases.reception: The council’s judgment in session XIII and the acclamations in session XVI name Honorius. Leo II expressly confirms the council and includes him in the anathema. The subsequent transmission to Spain explains his part in terms of failure to suppress error.
cases.contingency: Honorius’s directions on vocabulary concern how the bishops were to conduct a dispute. Constantinople III later defines the doctrine in that disputed vocabulary.
cases.development: The council defines two natural wills without opposition. Vatican I specifies the conditions of an ex cathedra act. The settled doctrinal content of each act can be compared with the historical judgment about Honorius.
cases.hypothesis: Honorius’s letters are official interventions whose meaning and consequences can be judged. They do not have the defining form and universal scope Vatican I requires. (T)
cases.objection: Honorius speaks doctrinally and asks other bishops to preach his position. An ecumenical council identifies his letters as confirming impious teaching. Is calling his reply a private opinion enough to reconcile the texts?
cases.rebuttal: His direction to other bishops establishes an official act. The further question under Pastor aeternus is whether he defined a doctrine to be held by the universal Church. His second reply directs bishops away from defining either formula for operations. The council’s strong judgment can be stated in full while recognizing the difference in the form and scope of the acts.

gaps.what: The best text of Leo II’s confirmation and the relation of its Latin and Greek versions
gaps.source: Riedinger, Acta Conciliorum Oecumenicorum, series II, vol. 2, part 2, and the relevant manuscript witnesses.
gaps.settles: Which wording was transmitted in each recension and how strongly the confirmation describes Honorius’s agency.

gaps.what: The extent to which the council’s judgment addressed Honorius’s intended meaning
gaps.source: The wider sequence of sessions XII–XVI, the controversial letters of Sergius and Cyrus, and John IV’s full letter.
gaps.settles: Whether the council’s concern was the stated proposition, the effect of suppressing a formula, or both.

cases.next_source: Collate the text of Leo II’s confirmation in Riedinger with the Mansi Latin and Greek and Leo’s letter to Spain.

audio.taught: Honorius wrote of one will and tried to quiet the dispute over operations. Constantinople Three condemned him and defined two natural wills and operations in Christ.
audio.authority: The council’s judgment gave a reason from the correspondence. Leo the Second confirmed the anathema. Vatican One defined infallibility for a specified act addressed to the whole Church.
audio.permanence: The dogmas on Christ and papal infallibility stand. The precise historical reading of Honorius and the wording of Leo’s confirmation still deserve study.

evidence_reviews.question: What does Honorius’s official correspondence say?
evidence_reviews.finding: The first letter says one will and invokes Christ’s freedom from fallen conflict. The second directs bishops to avoid one or two operations while confessing that each nature acts in the same Christ.
evidence_reviews.test: Compare both letters with John IV’s defense and with the later distinction between two natural wills and contrary wills.

evidence_reviews.question: What grounds did the council and Leo II actually give?
evidence_reviews.finding: The council says Honorius followed Sergius and confirmed impious doctrines. The Latin confirmation’s stronger expression and the Greek wording about allowing the faith to be stained are both transmitted. Leo’s letter to Spain expressly says negligence fostered the error.
evidence_reviews.test: Read the conciliar sentence, the confirmation, and the Spanish letter as distinct witnesses. Check the versions before deciding the precise meaning of the confirmation.

evidence_reviews.question: Do the letters meet Vatican I’s conditions?
evidence_reviews.finding: The letters address a doctrinal dispute and direct bishops. Their stated aim and audience give no evidence of a definition of doctrine to be held by the whole Church.
evidence_reviews.test: Apply the criteria to the stated action and addressees. The doctrinal subject and the pope’s official capacity do not establish the form or universal scope of a definition.

cases.title: John XXII's sermons and Benedictus Deus
cases.question: Were John XXII's sermons denying the immediate beatific vision before the judgment authoritative magisterium, private preaching, or something else?
cases.summary: In sermons of 1331–1332 John XXII argued that the souls of the blessed see Christ's humanity but not the divine essence until the last judgment. Theologians at Paris resisted; John said he was speaking as a theologian, offered to be corrected, and on the eve of his death (1334) retracted in the bull Ne super his. Benedict XII then defined in Benedictus Deus (1336) that the souls of the just see the divine essence immediately after death or purgation. John's sermons were not definitions; he expressly proposed them as opinion open to correction. The definition followed. John XXII's own texts are not yet on the site.

texts.label: John XXII, sermons (1331–1332) and Ne super his (3 December 1334)

propositions.says: The souls of the blessed do not see the divine essence until the general judgment.
John retracts, holding that purified souls see the divine essence clearly, as far as the state of a separated soul allows, and submits what he said to the Church's judgment.

propositions.quote: with apostolic authority we declare
propositions.says: The souls of the just, after death or purgation, see the divine essence by intuitive and face-to-face vision before the resumption of their bodies.

matrix.why: P and not-P in the same sense. But d3-j was proposed as opinion, retracted, and never defined, so no definition is contradicted.

cases.qualifications: John XXII spoke in sermons and repeatedly said he was open to correction (H, to be verified).
cases.reception: Cited at Vatican I by the minority; answered as private teaching. Some historians (e.g., Dykmans) stress that John pressed the opinion with his authority for several years.
cases.contingency: Not applicable.
cases.development: The definition of 1336 made explicit what was commonly held.
cases.hypothesis: The sermons were the opinion of a pope speaking as a theologian, not magisterial definitions; no definition was contradicted. (T)
cases.objection: A pope preached, publicly and repeatedly, a doctrine later defined as false, and pressed theologians to accept it; that is more than private opinion and shows that a pope's ordinary teaching can err in faith.
cases.rebuttal: It shows that a pope's non-definitive teaching can err, which Donum Veritatis 24 allows for in prudential interventions and which no definition excludes. It does not touch the conditions of Pastor aeternus 4.

gaps.what: John XXII's sermons and Ne super his
gaps.source: Dykmans, Les sermons de Jean XXII sur la vision béatifique (1973); DS 990–991
gaps.settles: How John qualified his teaching.

cases.next_source: Ne super his, in Denzinger–Hünermann.

audio.taught: Pope John XXII preached that the saints do not see God's essence until the last judgment, then took it back before he died. His successor Benedict XII defined that they see God face to face right after death or purification.
audio.authority: Sermons, proposed as opinion; a papal definition.
audio.permanence: Permanent: the beatific vision immediately after death or purgation. The sermons were an error of a pope teaching as a theologian.

cases.title: Apostolicae curae and later discussion of Anglican orders
cases.question: How are a doctrinal rule, the historical facts it applies to, the validity of a sacrament and later changed circumstances distinguished in Leo XIII's judgment on Anglican orders?
cases.summary: Leo XIII declared in 1896 that ordinations in the Anglican rite "have hitherto been and are invalid and entirely void", for defect of form and of intention. The 1998 commentary on the Profession of Faith gives this declaration as an example of a truth held definitively. Later discussion has asked whether ordinations in which bishops of undoubtedly valid orders took part (the "Dutch touch") change the facts. The rule (form and intention are required) is doctrine; the judgment on the Ordinal is a dogmatic fact; the validity of a particular later ordination is a question of fact about that ordination. A changed fact in a later case does not reverse the judgment on the rite. Anglicanorum Coetibus (2009) provides for the absolute ordination of former Anglican clergy, in line with 1896.

texts.label: Doctrine of the Faith, commentary on the Professio fidei, no. 11 (1998)

propositions.says: A sacrament requires matter and form that signify the grace they effect; in orders, the form must signify the order conferred.

propositions.quote: ordinations enacted according to the Anglican rite have hitherto been and are invalid and entirely void
propositions.says: Ordinations in the Anglican rite have been and are invalid and entirely void.
The declaration of Leo XIII on the invalidity of Anglican ordinations is an example of a truth to be held definitively.
propositions.ext: Commentary on the Professio fidei, no. 11

propositions.says: Old Catholic bishops, whose orders Rome recognises as valid, took part in some Anglican episcopal consecrations after 1932.

matrix.why: The judgment concerns the rite as it was and is; a later ordination with a valid co-consecrator raises a question of fact about that ordination, which the judgment does not decide.
The commentary places the declaration in the second paragraph of the Profession.

cases.qualifications: "Ordinations enacted according to the Anglican rite"; "hitherto been and are".
cases.reception: The Anglican archbishops replied in Saepius officio (1897). ARCIC suggested in 1985 that agreement on Eucharist and ministry created a "new context"; Cardinal Willebrands wrote in that sense. Rome has continued to ordain former Anglican clergy absolutely, and conditionally only in some individual cases.
cases.contingency: Applies to individual later ordinations, not to the judgment on the rite.
cases.development: What survives: the rule on form and intention; the judgment on the rite.
cases.hypothesis: A doctrinal rule applied to a historical rite in a dogmatic fact; later facts about particular ordinations are a separate question. (T)
cases.objection: The 1998 commentary's example is itself an authentic, non-definitive text; a dogmatic fact about a sixteenth-century rite rests on historical judgments (of intention) that are reformable.
cases.rebuttal: That is a fair objection to the grade, which the site records as definitive only on the commentary's authority (P7). It does not create a contradiction between the texts.

gaps.what: The 1998 commentary's list of examples in full
gaps.settles: The grade the Congregation gives.

cases.next_source: The 1998 commentary, no. 11.

audio.taught: Leo XIII declared that ordinations in the Anglican rite are invalid, because the rite did not express the priesthood and the intention to confer it.
audio.authority: A papal letter; the Doctrine of the Faith later gave it as an example of a truth held definitively.
audio.permanence: Permanent: the rule that form and intention are required, and the judgment on the rite. Open: questions of fact about particular later ordinations.

cases.title: Baptism, original sin and the limbo hypothesis
cases.question: How are a speculative theological conclusion (limbo), definitive propositions on baptism and original sin, and non-definitive hope for unbaptised infants to be distinguished?
cases.summary: Innocent III taught that the punishment of original sin is the loss of the vision of God. Florence taught that souls departing in original sin only go down at once to hell, to be punished with different penalties. Trent defined the necessity of infant baptism. Pius VI condemned the Jansenist charge that limbo is a Pelagian fable. The International Theological Commission (2007) found serious grounds to hope that unbaptised infants are saved, while calling limbo a still possible opinion. Limbo was never defined; Pius VI defended its admissibility, not its truth; the Commission's hope is non-definitive. What remains definitive is the necessity of baptism and the reality of original sin. The texts fit together at their grades.

texts.label: International Theological Commission, The Hope of Salvation for Infants Who Die Without Being Baptised (2007)

propositions.says: The souls of those who depart in actual mortal sin, or in original sin only, go down at once to hell, to be punished with different penalties.
Infants are to be baptised for the remission of sins; they contract original sin from Adam.

propositions.quote: rejects as a Pelagian fable
propositions.says: Condemned as false, rash and injurious to Catholic schools: the doctrine that rejects the limbo of children as a Pelagian fable.
There are serious theological and liturgical grounds for hope that unbaptised infants who die will be saved; limbo remains a possible theological opinion.

matrix.why: Florence: those dying in original sin only are punished. ITC: hope that unbaptised infants are saved. Concord if the hope rests on the possibility that God frees them from original sin by means unknown to us (so they do not die "in original sin only"); conflict if the hope is that they are saved while dying in it.
Pius VI defended limbo as a permitted opinion against the charge of Pelagianism; the ITC keeps it as a possible opinion.

cases.qualifications: Pius VI: censures of the lighter class ("false, rash, injurious to Catholic schools"). ITC: "hope", "not sure knowledge".
cases.reception: Cajetan and others had speculated about salvation through the parents' prayer; Trent declined to condemn him. The ITC text is a study authorised for publication, not a magisterial act.
cases.contingency: Not applicable.
cases.development: What survives: original sin, the necessity of baptism, the loss of the vision of God as its penalty. Open: whether God supplies for infants who die unbaptised.
cases.hypothesis: The hope is that God frees such infants from original sin in ways known to him, so that Florence's proposition does not apply to them; this keeps every definitive statement. (T)
cases.objection: Florence and the medieval teaching assume that unbaptised infants do die in original sin; the hope removes the case to which the dogma was meant to apply.
cases.rebuttal: The dogma says what happens to those who die in original sin; it does not define who in fact does. The objection is real against the claim that the hope is certain, which the ITC does not make.

gaps.what: The ITC document, nos. 40–41, 70, 102–103
gaps.source: vatican.va (2007)
gaps.settles: How the Commission relates its hope to Florence.

audio.taught: The Church teaches that original sin is real and baptism is necessary. Florence taught that those who die in original sin alone are deprived of heaven. Pius VI defended the idea of limbo against the charge of heresy. A theological commission in 2007 found serious grounds to hope that unbaptised infants are saved.
audio.authority: Conciliar definitions; a papal censure; a study by a theological commission.
audio.permanence: Permanent: original sin and the necessity of baptism. Never defined: limbo. Hope, not certainty: the salvation of these infants.

cases.title: Trent and later disciplinary norms on Communion
cases.question: What in Trent's teaching on Communion is divine law about the sacrament, and what is positive ecclesiastical discipline?
cases.summary: Constance defined that Christ is wholly present under each species and upheld Communion under one kind as a reasonable custom. Basel allowed the chalice to the Hussites on condition that they taught the same doctrine; Pius II revoked the concession. Trent defined that the faithful are not bound by divine law to receive under both kinds, that the Church had just reasons to give one kind, and that Christ is received whole under either, and left the granting of the chalice to the pope. Vatican II allowed Communion under both kinds in cases set by the Holy See. Doctrine: the whole Christ under each species; the Church's power over the manner of distribution. Discipline: whether to give the chalice. Every change concerns the second.

propositions.says: Although Christ instituted the sacrament under both species, the custom of giving the laity one species is reasonable; Christ is wholly under each.
Anathema to whoever says that every one of the faithful is bound by divine precept or necessity of salvation to receive both species.

propositions.quote: has not been influenced by just causes and reasons to give communion under the form of bread only
propositions.says: Anathema to whoever says the Church lacked just causes for giving Communion under one kind, or erred in it.
Basel allows the chalice to the Utraquists on condition that they teach Christ is whole under each kind; Pius II revokes it (1462).
The dogmatic principles of Trent remaining intact, Communion under both kinds may be granted in cases to be determined by the Holy See.

matrix.why: Trent: the Church had just reasons for one kind and did not err. Vatican II: the Church may give both kinds in determined cases. Both affirm the Church's power over the manner; neither says the other practice is wrong.
A concession of the chalice joined to the doctrine that it is not necessary; its revocation changed discipline only.

cases.qualifications: Sacrosanctum Concilium 55: "the dogmatic principles which were laid down by the Council of Trent remaining intact".
cases.reception: Utraquism persisted in Bohemia; Pius IV granted the chalice to some German dioceses in 1564 and later withdrew it. Later norms (the Eucharistic fast, Communion in the hand) are discussed in the disputed question on other changed disciplines.
cases.contingency: Passes: the manner of distribution is a contingent determination; Trent itself says so.
cases.development: What survives: the whole Christ under each species; the Church's power over the sacraments "salva illorum substantia" (n. 931).
cases.hypothesis: Divine law: the real presence of the whole Christ under each kind, and the Church's power over the manner of administration. Discipline: the chalice. (D)
cases.objection: Trent defended one kind with "just causes", and those causes (danger of irreverence, error about the whole Christ) have not changed; restoring the chalice disregards a judgment the council anathematised anyone for calling erroneous.
cases.rebuttal: The canon anathematises saying the Church erred in giving one kind, not giving both kinds where she judges it fitting; Trent itself left the chalice to the pope. The objection is a prudential one, which the texts allow.
